question: A 54-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with unsightly toenails affecting the lateral three nails of the left foot. On examination the nails and brown and break easily. Nail scrapings demonstrate Trichophyton rubrum infection. What is the treatment of choice?
explanation:
Dermatophyte nail infections - use oral terbinafine

The correct answer is

Oral terbinafine for 12 weeks

. This is because oral terbinafine is the first-line treatment for onychomycosis (fungal nail infection) caused by dermatophytes such as

Trichophyton rubrum

. A 12-week course of oral terbinafine is recommended for toenail infections, as they take longer to treat than fingernail infections due to slower nail growth.

Oral itraconazole for 4 weeks

is incorrect because, although itraconazole can be used as an alternative treatment for onychomycosis, a 4-week course would not be sufficient to treat a toenail infection. Itraconazole is typically given in a pulsed dosing regimen, where the patient takes the medication daily for one week per month. For toenail infections, this regimen should be continued for at least three months.

Topical itraconazole for 2 weeks

is not an appropriate choice because topical antifungal agents are generally less effective than oral medications in treating onychomycosis. Additionally, there are no UK guidelines recommending the use of topical itraconazole specifically for this condition.

Topical amorolfine for 6 weeks

is also incorrect because topical treatments are typically reserved for mild cases of onychomycosis or when oral medications cannot be used due to contraindications or side effects. In this case, the patient has multiple affected nails and a confirmed

T. rubrum

infection, making oral therapy more suitable. Furthermore, if amorolfine were chosen as a topical treatment option, a longer duration of therapy (up to six months) would be required.

Finally,

Oral itraconazole for 1 week

is not a suitable treatment option because, as discussed earlier, itraconazole should be given in a pulsed dosing regimen for at least three months to effectively treat toenail onychomycosis. A 1-week course would not provide adequate treatment duration to eradicate the fungal infection.

question:
A 24-year-old man presents with a swollen, itchy right eyelid. This has been ongoing for 10 days but the patient reports it has happened at least 5 times previously. Each time it self-resolved.

On examination, there is erythema of the anterior lid margin and the base of the lashes of the right eye. Visual acuity, fundoscopy and cranial nerve examination are normal.

You perform a systematic enquiry to elicit an underlying cause of this recurrent condition.

What is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
Otitis externa and blepharitis are common complications of seborrhoeic dermatitis

This is a history and examination suggesting anterior blepharitis. The most common underlying cause is

seborrhoeic dermatitis

. Seborrhoeic dermatitis normally causes eczematous lesions in the scalp, periorbital, auricular and nasolabial folds. It also can lead to otitis externa.

Atopic dermatitis

(otherwise called atopic eczema) is the most common inflammatory skin condition. It can affect the face more commonly in childhood but does not commonly lead to blepharitis. Important complications of atopic dermatitis include staphylococcal infection and eczema herpeticum.

Psoriasis

does not typically cause blepharitis or any eye pathology. Complications of psoriasis include arthropathy as well as increased incidence of metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease and venous thromboembolism.

Rheumatoid arthritis

does not commonly cause blepharitis. However, ocular manifestations are common and include keratoconjunctivitis sicca, episcleritis, scleritis, corneal ulceration and keratitis. The examination findings in this question are not suggestive of any of these.

Rosacea

is a condition causing flushing, telangiectasia, erythema and pustules of the face. It is a recognised cause of blepharitis but would be less common than seborrhoeic dermatitis in a 24-year-old male.

question: A 43-year-old woman is referred to psychiatry following repeated episodes of hypomaniac behaviour interspersed with periods of depression. Her past medical history includes psoriasis and a deep vein thrombosis 11 years ago. Which one of the following medications is most likely to worsen her psoriasis?
explanation:
Psoriasis: lithium may trigger an exacerbation

The correct answer in this case is

Lithium

. Lithium is known to exacerbate psoriasis in some patients. The exact mechanism by which lithium worsens psoriasis is not completely understood, but it is thought to be related to its effects on the immune system and skin cell proliferation. Lithium can cause an increase in the production of certain cytokines that play a role in the development of psoriasis, as well as directly stimulate keratinocyte proliferation.

The other options are less likely to worsen psoriasis:

Sodium valproate

and

Valproaic acid

(which are essentially the same medication) are anticonvulsant medications that can also be used as mood stabilisers for patients with bipolar disorder. While they do have some immunomodulatory effects, there is no strong evidence to suggest that they significantly exacerbate psoriasis. In fact, some studies have suggested that valproate may even have a beneficial effect on psoriasis due to its anti-inflammatory properties.

Quetiapine

is an atypical antipsychotic medication that can also be used as a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder. There have been isolated case reports of quetiapine-induced psoriasis; however, these are rare occurrences and not considered a common side effect of the medication. Overall, quetiapine is less likely than lithium to worsen psoriasis.

Finally,

Fluoxetine

is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant medication. Although SSRIs can potentially cause various skin reactions, including rash and pruritus, there is no consistent evidence linking fluoxetine specifically with the worsening of psoriasis.

question: A 52-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman presents to the dermatology department. She has noticed a patch of pigmented skin on her toe, which has been slowly enlarging over the past five months. On examination, she has pigmentation of the nail bed of her great toe, affecting the adjacent cuticle and proximal nail fold. Which subtype of melanoma would you expect to present in this manner?
explanation:
Acral lentiginous melanoma: Pigmentation of nail bed affecting proximal nail fold suggests melanoma (Hutchinson's sign)

Acral lentiginous melanoma is the rarest form of melanoma overall, but the commonest form of melanoma in people with darker skin. Hence it is important to be able to recognise.

Acral lentiginous melanoma mostly affects people over the age of 40 and is equally common in males and females. It is not related to sun exposure. It typically presents as an enlarging discoloured skin patch on the palms, fingers, soles or toes with the characteristics of other flat forms of melanoma. It can arise in the nail unit, appearing as general discolouration or irregular pigmented bands running longitudinally along the nail plate and is called subungual melanoma when it arises in the matrix.

This patient has subungual acral lentiginous melanoma with an important clinical clue of this called 'Hutchinson's nail sign'.  This sign is characterised by extension of the nail bed, matrix and nail plate pigmentation to the adjacent cuticle and proximal or lateral nail folds.

The other forms of melanoma are less likely to present in this way and are described in more detail in the notes below.

question:
A 26-year-old woman has been referred to the dermatology clinic with a 4-week history of skin rash.

Past medical history includes mild asthma. Regular medications include folic acid 400micrograms OD and over-the-counter vitamin supplements due to pregnancy.

She feels well in herself but states she had a mild cold when the lesions first developed.

On examination, she has multiple, discrete, raised erythematous lesions on the arms and legs ranging from 8cm in diameter to 12cm in diameter. There is pain on active and passive joint movement.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum may be caused by pregnancy

The above scenario holds multiple crucial pieces of information that combined give the correct answer of

erythema nodosum

. Erythema nodosum typically lasts for 4-6 weeks, can develop after a flu-like illness, is associated with multiple erythematous lesions affecting the limbs, and is associated with pregnancy. Lesions are often nodular and tender, and the rash is self-terminating. It is often accompanied by arthralgia.

Erythema ab igne

is a reticulated rash caused by over-exposure to infrared radiation. It commonly occurs in people with high levels of exposure to heat such as fireplaces and hot water bottles. It is not associated with recent illness and there are no discrete lesions.

As with erythema nodosum,

erythema marginatum

is a skin rash that commonly affects the limbs. However, the lesions are typically circular with a raised outer area and pale center and also affect the torso. It is associated with multiple conditions, most commonly rheumatic fever and group A Streptococcus. It is not associated with pregnancy.

Erythema migrans

is the classic Lyme disease rash appearing in 80% of Lyme disease cases. It appears as a 'bull's eye' rash with a red outer circle, pale inner circle, and red center.

An

erythema multiforme

rash initially appears as red patches on the hands before progressing to target lesions. It is associated with many infections including bacterial, viral, and fungal, and is thought to be an immune-mediated reaction.

question: A 64-year-old woman presents with severe mucosal ulceration associated with the development of blistering lesions over her torso and arms. On examination the blisters are flaccid and easily ruptured when touched. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Blisters/bullae

The most likely diagnosis, in this case, is

Pemphigus vulgaris

. This condition is characterized by the presence of flaccid blisters and mucosal ulceration, which are easily ruptured when touched. Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disorder caused by autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 and 3, which are proteins responsible for maintaining the integrity of keratinocyte adhesion in the epidermis. The loss of adhesion leads to intraepidermal blister formation.

Pemphigoid

is another autoimmune blistering disorder, but it differs from pemphigus vulgaris in that it involves the formation of tense blisters rather than flaccid ones. In pemphigoid, autoantibodies target components of the basement membrane zone, leading to subepidermal blister formation. Due to the deeper location of these blisters compared to those seen in pemphigus vulgaris, they are more resistant to rupture.

Dermatitis herpetiformis

is a chronic autoimmune skin condition associated with gluten sensitivity and coeliac disease. It presents as intensely pruritic papules, vesicles, and excoriations typically distributed symmetrically on extensor surfaces such as elbows, knees, and buttocks. Although it can present with blisters, these tend to be small and clustered rather than large and flaccid like those seen in pemphigus vulgaris.

Psoriasis

is a common chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales. It does not typically present with blistering or mucosal involvement as seen in this patient's presentation.

Epidermolysis bullosa

refers to a group of rare inherited disorders characterized by fragility of the skin and mucous membranes leading to blister formation. These blisters can be induced by minor trauma or friction, but the onset of symptoms is usually in infancy or early childhood, making it an unlikely diagnosis for a 64-year-old woman presenting with new-onset blistering lesions.

question:
A 27-year-old man attends his GP complaining of a rash. On closer inspection, there are extensive pink umbilicated lesions visible on his trunk and around his wrists. Some of these are itchy. Observations are all within normal limits. The GP requests an HIV test which comes back as positive.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Extensive umbilicated lesions in HIV - molluscum contagiosum

This is a typical description of molluscum contagiosum. The majority of cases occur in children, however, extensive lesions in an HIV-positive person warrants an urgent referral to an HIV specialist. Although these lesions are typically non-painful, they can sometimes be itchy.

Scabies is a skin infestation caused by a mite. They reproduce on the surface of your skin and then burrow into it and lay eggs. This causes an incredibly itchy, red rash to form on the skin, which is often exacerbated by scratching.

It is important to consider shingles in immunocompromised patients. However, the rash is likely to be painful, with blisters in a localized area (typically a dermatomal distribution).

Kaposi's sarcoma is a cancer that forms purple lesions (flat or raised) on the skin. It is commonly seen in immunocompromised patients and is an AIDS-defining illness.

Prurigo nodularis is a skin disorder that causes hard, itchy nodules to form on the skin. The itching may be so severe that it leads to people scratching themselves to the point of bleeding or pain.

question:
A 56-year-old man presents with a lesion on his right lower leg. He states that it has been growing in size over the last 3 months. On examination, you note a 2x3cm ulcerated crusted lump over the right anterior shin.

A CT scan is performed:


CT neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis	No evidence of regional lymph node involvement or distant metastases

What treatment is indicated given the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A non-healing painless ulcer associated with a chronic scar is indicative of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)

The diagnosis is most likely squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). A skin biopsy would be required to confirm the diagnosis before initiating treatment.

Surgical excision

is correct. Surgical excision is the preferred treatment for localised disease.  Surgical excision with 4mm margins is preferred if the lesion is <20mm in diameter, and with 6mm margins if the lesion is >20mm in diameter.

Chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy

is incorrect. Although initial surgical excision cures 95% of patients, a minority of cutaneous SCCs are considered unresectable, either locally advanced or with unresectable regional lymph nodes or distant metastases. These patients are offered systemic treatments with chemo-immunotherapy. Two checkpoint inhibitors, cemiplimab and pembrolizumab, have demonstrated a high response rate and survival with fewer toxicities than other available systemic agents. The CT scan in this case did not demonstrate any regional lymph node involvement or distant metastases and thus systemic treatment can be avoided if the lesion can be fully resected.

Cryotherapy

is incorrect. Cryotherapy is used for some early squamous cell cancers, especially in people who can not have surgery. Superficial, in situ, or SCC less and equal to 1 cm has been successfully treated with cryosurgery with results comparable to traditional surgical excision. In this case, the lesion is > 1cm and therefore surgery is required.

Diclofenac topical gel

is incorrect. This can be used to treat actinic keratosis (the most common precursor lesion for squamous cell carcinoma). Actinic keratosis may be solitary but there are often multiple keratoses. The appearance varies. However, classically they present with flat to slightly raised, scaly, and crusty lesions which sometimes have a raised horn shape or bump. They usually occur on sun exposure sites (e.g. the scalp). In this case, the presence of ulceration favours a diagnosis of SCC.

Mohs micrographic surgery

is incorrect. Mohs micrographic surgery may be used in high-risk patients and in cosmetically important sites (e.g. face). Mohs surgery is designed to minimise scarring at the outset, by creating the smallest post-surgical wound possible.

question: A 22-year-old male is referred to dermatology clinic with a longstanding problem of bilateral excessive axillary sweating. He is otherwise well but the condition is affecting his confidence and limiting his social life. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Topical aluminium chloride preparations are first-line for hyperhidrosis

The most appropriate management for this 22-year-old male with bilateral excessive axillary sweating is the use of

topical aluminium chloride

. This condition is known as primary axillary hyperhidrosis, and topical aluminium chloride is the first-line treatment. It works by blocking the sweat ducts, thereby reducing the amount of sweat produced. This can significantly improve the patient's symptoms and quality of life.

A

non-sedating antihistamine

would not be an effective treatment for primary axillary hyperhidrosis. Antihistamines are typically used to manage allergic conditions such as urticaria or hay fever, where histamine plays a significant role in causing symptoms. In this case, there is no indication that histamine is involved in the patient's excessive sweating.

Topical hydrocortisone 1%

is also not an appropriate treatment option in this case. Hydrocortisone is a mild topical corticosteroid used to treat inflammatory skin conditions such as eczema or dermatitis. It has no role in managing excessive sweating caused by primary axillary hyperhidrosis.

Performing

thyroid function tests

may be considered if there was suspicion of an underlying thyroid disorder causing secondary hyperhidrosis; however, given the patient's age and presentation with isolated excessive axillary sweating without any other systemic symptoms suggestive of thyroid dysfunction, it is unlikely that thyroid function tests would be useful in this case.

A

trial of desmopressin

, a synthetic vasopressin analogue, would not be indicated for treating primary axillary hyperhidrosis. Desmopressin is used primarily for managing central diabetes insipidus or nocturnal enuresis due to its antidiuretic effects on renal collecting ducts. It does not have any direct effect on sweat production or the sweat glands.

question:
A 37-year-old woman, currently 36 weeks pregnant with her second child, has developed an itchy rash on the lower third of her abdomen. She reports they initially appeared as small pink spots over her stretch marks.

On examination, she has multiple large, erythematous plaques over her lower abdomen. Similar lesions also appear to be forming over her thighs. Her heart rate is 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 118/66 mmHg and she is afebrile.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is not associated with blistering

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy

develops in the third trimester and is characterised by the development of pruritic papules, often over abdominal striae, that evolve into larger erythematous plaques and may also spread to the buttocks and thighs. Treatment would involve emollients and topical steroids. Consider oral steroids if particularly widespread.

Atopic eruption of pregnancy

involves the development of a pruritic, eczematous rash, in the typical distribution seen in eczema. It is the most common skin problem in pregnancy, often presenting in the first or second trimester but may also present in the third. It often does not require specific treatment. The rash in this question does not have the eczematous distribution expected in the atopic eruption of pregnancy, and the evolution of pruritic papules to erythematous plaques is more characteristic of polymorphic eruption of pregnancy.

Bullous pemphigoid

is an autoimmune condition characterised by a tense blistering rash, most commonly seen in the elderly population. It can often be complicated by secondary bacterial or viral infection. The age, normal observations and lack of blistering make this very unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Pemphigoid gestationis

is characterised by pruritic, blistering lesions, initially periumbilical but later spreading to affect the rest of the torso and arms over weeks. It is most often seen in the second or third trimester, or early postpartum, and in subsequent pregnancies may present sooner. Treatment would involve steroids but may require immunosuppression if severe. It is unlikely in this case due to the lack of blistering and distribution of lesions.

Pemphigus vulgaris

is characterised by the formation of sometimes painful, fragile blisters, particularly on mucous membranes and may be complicated by secondary infection. Patients tend to be aged between 30-60 and it may be idiopathic, drug-induced, less commonly paraneoplastic or secondary to trauma or infection. Treat initially with systemic steroids.

question:
A 38-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a recurring itchy rash on his hands and feet. He frequently travels to the middle east on business. He has had unprotected sex recently on one of these trips.

On examination, there is an itchy vesicular rash on the palms and soles with areas of excoriation and erythema.

Exposure to what factor is the likely precipitant of this particular rash?
explanation:
Pompholyx eczema may be precipitated by humidity (e.g. sweating) and high temperatures

Humidity

is correct. The description of the rash (recurrent vesicles affecting the palms and soles associated with erythema) is typical of pompholyx eczema. This can be precipitated by humidity. His frequent travel to the middle east, which is an especially humid region, may be contributory.

Chlamydia

is incorrect. Keratoderma blennorrhagica may be precipitated by chlamydia in the context of reactive arthritis. This rash is found on the soles of the feet but can also affect the palms. It can be vesico-pustular but tends to have a waxy brown appearance rather than being erythematous and itchy.

Cold

is incorrect. This may precipitate Raynaud's phenomenon but not pompholyx eczema.

Sunlight

is incorrect. This can precipitate many conditions such as lupus and polymorphic light eruption. However, it is humidity rather than sunlight that precipitates pompholyx.

Syphilis

is incorrect. This can cause a rash on the palms and soles but it is typically macular.

question: A 25-year-old man presents with a widespread rash over his body. The torso and limbs are covered with multiple erythematous lesions less than 1 cm in diameter which in parts are covered by a fine scale. You note that two weeks earlier he was seen with a sore throat when it was noted that he had exudative tonsillitis. Other than a history of asthma he is normally fit and well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute onset of tear-drop scaly papules on trunk and limbs → ?guttate psoriasis

The correct answer is

guttate psoriasis

. Guttate psoriasis is a type of psoriasis that presents as small, erythematous papules and plaques with fine scaling, often triggered by a preceding streptococcal infection such as tonsillitis. In this case, the patient's recent history of exudative tonsillitis, along with the description of the rash involving the torso and limbs with erythematous lesions and fine scale, strongly supports the diagnosis of guttate psoriasis.

Pityriasis rosea

is an incorrect answer because although it can present with a widespread rash on the trunk and limbs, it typically begins with a single larger 'herald patch' followed by smaller oval-shaped lesions that have a collarette scale. Moreover, pityriasis rosea is not associated with preceding streptococcal infections.

Pityriasis versicolor

(also known as tinea versicolor) is another incorrect option. This condition is caused by an overgrowth of

Malassezia

yeasts on the skin and presents as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented scaly patches typically found on the upper trunk. The distribution and appearance of this patient's rash do not fit with pityriasis versicolor.

Syphilis

is also an incorrect choice in this scenario. While secondary syphilis can cause a widespread rash that may involve the palms and soles, it usually presents as non-pruritic maculopapular lesions without scaling. Additionally, other symptoms such as fever, lymphadenopathy, or mucosal involvement would be expected in secondary syphilis.

Finally,

discoid eczema

, also known as nummular dermatitis or discoid dermatitis, is not consistent with this patient's presentation. Discoid eczema presents as coin-shaped, pruritic, erythematous patches with scaling and crusting, typically on the limbs. The patient's history of preceding tonsillitis and the description of the rash make guttate psoriasis a more likely diagnosis.

question:
A 4-year-old child, born in a refugee camp, is brought to the health clinic with clear evidence of malnutrition. The child has a characteristic rash with red crusted lesions in acral, periorificial and perianal distribution.

Other clinical features include poor growth and cognitive development.

What deficiency is most associated with this child's presentation?
explanation:
Dermatitis in acral, peri-orificial and perianal distribution → ?zinc deficiency

This child has presented with acrodermatitis, a rash with red, crusted lesions affecting the acral distribution (the distal portion of the limbs i.e. hands, foot, and head i.e. ears, nose), periorificial and perianal distributions. Acquired acrodermatitis is a result of

zinc

deficiency due to reduced intake, increased zinc demands, malabsorption or rarely secondary to metabolic disorders. Primary acrodermatitis (also referred to as primary acrodermatitis enteropathica) is an inherited condition resulting in reduced intestinal zinc absorption secondary to a zinc transport defect. Other features of zinc deficiency include alopecia, night blindness, cognitive impairment and growth issues.

Iodine

deficiency mainly results in thyroid issues with iodine being needed to produce thyroxine. Iodine deficiency, therefore, results in hypothyroidism and a characteristic swelling of the thyroid gland known as a goitre. Iodine deficiency can also result in hair loss and skin changes in the form of myxoedema, which is a waxy, discoloured induration of the skin, generally affecting the pretibial areas.

Magnesium

deficiency can result in multiple signs including tremors, muscle cramping, and muscle spasming. It can also result in nervous system dysfunctions, cardiac dysrhythmias and personality changes. In general skin changes and specific rashes are not associated with magnesium deficiency.

Niacin (vitamin B3)

deficiency results in pellagra, a condition that classically results in the fours D's, diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia and eventually death. Skin changes in pellagra are common but are generally seen as a darkening and stiffening of the skin which may peel or bleed. A specific broad collar rash known as Casal collar is also associated with the condition, resulting in an erythematous, pigmented rash in the broad collar distribution (dermatomes C3 and C4).

Vitamin A

deficiency generally affects the eyes and is the commonest cause of blindness in low-income countries. Vitamin A is an important component of rhodopsin found in the retina and deficiency results in nyctalopia (night blindness), xerophthalmia (drying of the eyes), keratomalacia and eventually complete blindness. Skin changes are not commonly associated with vitamin A deficiency.

question: Which one of the following factors would predispose a patient to forming keloid scars?
options: Incisions along relaxed skin tension lines
Having a wound on the lower back
explanation:
Keloid scars - more common in young, black, male adults

The correct answer is

Being aged 20-40 years

. Keloid scars are a result of an overactive healing process where the body produces excess collagen, leading to raised and often itchy or painful scars. They are more common in individuals aged 10-30 years old, with a peak incidence between 20-40 years. This is because younger skin has a higher capacity for cellular proliferation and therefore tends to heal faster and produce more collagen.

Having white skin

is not a predisposing factor for keloid formation. In fact, keloids are less common in people with lighter skin types. Darker-skinned individuals, especially those of African, Hispanic or Asian descent, have a higher risk of developing keloids due to genetic factors.

Incisions along relaxed skin tension lines

actually decrease the likelihood of keloid formation. These lines represent the natural orientation of collagen fibres in the dermis. Surgical incisions made along these lines result in less tension on wound edges during healing, reducing the risk of abnormal scar formation including keloids.

Being female

, while may increase the likelihood of hypertrophic scarring (another type of raised scar), does not specifically predispose to keloid formation. Both sexes can develop keloids, though some studies suggest a slight female predominance which could be attributed to practices like ear piercing rather than biological sex itself.

Finally,

having a wound on the lower back

is not particularly associated with an increased risk of keloid formation compared to other locations on the body. However, areas with high levels of tension such as sternum, shoulders and earlobes are known hotspots for keloids due to constant movement and stretching that can stimulate excessive collagen production during healing.

question:
A 53-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 1-week history of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and flushing. She reports burning epigastric pain and she is passing 3 to 5 loose bowel motions a day.

On examination, she has epigastric tenderness, however, her abdomen is soft with no rigidity, guarding or distension. She has innumerable reddish-brown papules on her trunk. It is noted that when gentle friction is applied to the rash an urticarial reaction is observed.

Further investigations reveal raised serum tryptase and urinary histamine levels.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 54-year-old man presents to his GP with a rash.

On examination, he has several well-demarcated purple papules on his forearms. The papules have thin visible white lines running across them. The patient describes the lesions as very itchy, but not painful, and is keen to know if there is anything that can help with the symptoms.

What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Potent topical steroids are the first-line treatment for lichen planus

Topical steroids

is correct. The rash described is lichen planus, characterized by itchy purple polygonal papules. The white lines are Wickham's striae. Lichen planus can persist for up to 18 months, and topical steroids are the first-line treatment.

Oral steroids

is incorrect. The itching of lichen planus usually responds well to topical steroids. Oral steroids may be required in severe or extensive disease, but this is not seen here.

No treatment required

is incorrect. While lichen planus may resolve spontaneously, it can take up to 18 months and this patient is asking for help with the symptoms of itching. Topical steroids is therefore the correct option.

Topical retinoids

is incorrect. The rash described here is lichen planus. Topical retinoids are used in acne vulgaris.

Topical vitamin D analogues

is incorrect. The rash described here is lichen planus. Topical vitamin D analogues are used in plaque psoriasis.

question: Each one of the following is associated with hypertrichosis, except:

A 28-year-old car mechanic presented with symptoms of itchy blisters on his palms, fingers and soles of his feet. Over the past few days, they have become intensely itchy to the point where he struggles to sleep at night. He reports that his work has become very stressful recently and the summer heat means he is sweating more too.

What is the most likely skin condition in this case?
explanation:
Pompholyx eczema may be precipitated by humidity (e.g. sweating) and high temperatures

Pompholyx (also known as dyshidrotic eczema) is a type of eczema which causes tiny blisters to arise across the fingers, palms of the hands and in some cases the soles of the feet. It commonly affects adults under 40 years old. The exact causes of pompholyx eczema are unknown, but factors such as stress, sensitivity to metal compounds e.g. nickel or cobalt, sweating can aggravate it.

Discoid eczema is a common type of eczema/dermatitis defined by scattered, well-defined, coin-shaped and coin-sized plaques of eczema. Blisters occur less commonly meaning it is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Palmoplantar hyperhidrosis is a common condition in which sweat glands of the palms and soles produce inappropriately large quantities of sweat, worse in warmer weather. Blisters occur less commonly meaning it is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

Palmoplantar pustulosis is an autoimmune disorder marked by the appearance of fluid-filled pustules or blisters on the hands and feet and is considered to be a variant of psoriasis. The pustules may be painful and cause a burning feeling, which is not the case here.

Palmoplantar keratoderma is a skin condition characterised by thickening of the skin on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, which is not described here.

question: A 38-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis and epilepsy presents with generalised increased hair growth over her trunk and arms. Which one of the following drugs is associated with hypertrichosis?

A 58-year-old woman presents with a persistent erythematous rash on her cheeks and a 'red nose'. She describes occasional episodes of facial flushing. On examination erythematous skin is noted on the nose and cheeks associated with occasional papules. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Rosacea: topical ivermectin is first-line for patients mild papules and/or pustules

Given that this woman has mild symptoms, topical ivermectin should be used first line

question: A 34-year-old man presents for the removal of a mole. Where on the body are keloid scars most likely to form?
explanation:
Keloid scars are most common on the sternum

The correct answer is the

sternum

. Keloid scars are a result of an overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue that usually develops after the healing of a skin injury. The scar extends beyond the borders of the original wound, does not regress and tends to recur after excision. The sternum, along with other areas such as shoulders, upper arms and earlobes, is particularly prone to keloid formation due to high tension in these areas.

The

lower back

, although it can develop keloid scars, is not as commonly affected as the sternum. This may be due to less tension in this area compared to the chest wall or less frequent injury.

Keloids can also form on the

abdomen

, but they are not as common in this location as on the sternum. It's important to note that surgical incisions, such as those for abdominal surgeries, can lead to keloid formation if the individual has a predisposition.

The

flexor surfaces of limbs

are less likely to form keloids compared to other parts of the body because these areas are usually covered by clothing and therefore protected from trauma. However, piercings or burns in these areas could potentially lead to keloid formation.

Lastly, while it's possible for keloids to develop on the

scalp

, they're relatively rare in this location. This could be due to several factors including fewer injuries occurring on this part of the body or perhaps related to differences in hair follicle biology which may influence wound healing and scar formation.

question: A 62-year-old female is referred to dermatology due to a lesion over her shin. It initially started as a small red papule which later became a deep, red, necrotic ulcer with a violaceous border. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 43-year-old presents with itchy lesions on the soles of both feet. These have been present for the past two months. On examination small blisters are seen with surrounding dry and cracked skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 17-year-old female was admitted with a fever and an acute wide-spread rash. She has a background of atopic eczema affecting her extensor surfaces and face. On examination, she has monomorphous erythematous vesicles with some lesions having eroded and crusted, on her face, extensor surfaces, as well as palms and soles, and oral ulcers. A viral swab was sent for herpes simplex (HSV-1 and HSV-2) and varicella-zoster viruses were negative. She has developed new lesions despite treatment with acyclovir.

What is the likely viral cause of this patient's rash?
explanation:
Eczema herpeticum is a primary infection of the skin caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) and uncommonly coxsackievirus

Coxsackie virus

can cause 'eczema coxsackium', which is a key differential for eczema herpeticum. It is usually a self-limiting infection that does not respond to treatment with acyclovir.

Cytomegalovirus

is a member of the Herpesviridae family (HHV-5) and rarely causes cutaneous symptoms, but when it does it is usually localised.

Epstein-Barr virus

is a member of the Herpesviridae family (HHV-4) and often causes a morbilliform rash following administration of a penicillin antibiotic.

Human Herpesvirus-6

usually causes a mild disease in childhood frequently presenting as roseola. Primary infection in young adults is exceedingly rare, and do not feature a significant rash.

Human Herpesvirus-8

is the cause of Kaposi's sarcoma in the immunocompromised host, and possibly Castleman's disease in the immunocompetent adult. Primary infection in adults features mild symptoms and only a localised rash. In children, the primary infection may cause a fever and maculopapular rash.

question: A 43-year-old man comes for review. A few months ago he developed redness around his nose and cheeks. This is worse after drinking alcohol. He is concerned as one of his work colleagues asked him if he had a drink problem despite him drinking 14 units per week. On examination he has erythema as described above with some pustules on the nose and telangiectasia on the cheeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Rosacea features:

The correct answer is

Acne rosacea

. This condition is a chronic skin disease that often begins with a tendency to blush or flush more easily than others. The redness can slowly spread beyond the nose and cheeks to the forehead and chin. Even the ears, chest, and back can be red all the time. Acne rosacea presents as central facial erythema, telangiectasia (visible blood vessels), inflammatory lesions (papules and pustules) which this patient has. Alcohol is known to worsen rosacea though it does not cause it.

Mitral stenosis

is incorrect because it primarily affects the heart, specifically the mitral valve, causing symptoms such as breathlessness on exertion, palpitations, fatigue and oedema but not skin changes like those described in this question.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis

is incorrect as well. While it does affect the skin and may present with redness and flaking skin, its primary locations are areas rich in oil glands such as the scalp, eyebrows, sides of the nose, behind ears; unlike acne rosacea which prominently affects mid-face.

The option

Alcohol-related skin changes

might seem plausible given that alcohol exacerbates his condition; however, these typically include jaundice due to liver disease or superficial spider angiomas rather than pustules or persistent erythema like in this case.

Lastly,

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

, a systemic autoimmune disease, can indeed cause a malar rash ('butterfly' rash) over cheeks but this tends to be photosensitive rather than alcohol sensitive. Furthermore SLE associated rash usually spares nasolabial folds which seems unlikely here given pustules are present on his nose.

question:
A 40-year-old man with known end-stage renal failure has been on peritoneal dialysis for the past 5 years.

Family screening for a possible donor identified a potential match with his brother and following appropriate counselling a successful renal transplant was performed. On his 3-monthly review, there is no evidence of graft rejection.

What malignancy is this patient most at risk of in the future?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
correctText: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
explanation:
Renal transplant patients - skin cancer (particularly squamous cell) is the most common malignancy secondary to immunosuppression

All patients who undergo renal transplantation must be commenced and remain on immunosuppression therapy for the rest of their life to prevent the risk of transplant rejection. As an adverse effect, this immunosuppression therapy results in patients having an increased risk of carcinomas as their immune system is less able to identify and destroy newly formed cancer cells or prevent infections that may cause cancer.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin

has been shown to be the most common malignancy associated with immunosuppression.

Adenocarcinoma of the bowel

is the commonest form of colorectal cancer. Although its incidence, like most cancers, is increased in immunosuppressed patients there are several other risks factor associated with this cancer including dietary imbalances, smoking and a lack of physical exercise. As such colorectal cancer is less common in immunosuppressed patients when compared to other cancers.

Adenocarcinoma of the prostate

is mainly associated with obesity, hypertension and elevated testosterone levels. There is an increased risk of this form of cancer in immunosuppressed patients however it is not the commonest associated cancer.

B-cell lymphoma

is the group of blood and lymph tumours that develop from the B lymphocytes including both Hodgkin's and most non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Although there is an increased risk of lymphoma in patients on immunosuppression their incidence remains low.

The association between immunosuppression and

chronic lymphocytic leukaemia

(CLL) is not fully understood and although an increased risk may exist, the incidence of CLL in these patients is lower than other cancers.

question: A 62-year-old woman mentions in diabetes clinic that she has a 'volcano' like spot on her left cheek, which has appeared over the past 3 months. She initially thought it may be a simple spot but it has not gone away. On examination she has a 5 mm red, raised lesion with a central keratin filled crater. A clinical diagnosis of probable keratoacanthoma is made. What is the most suitable management?
options: Reassure will spontaneously involute within 3 months

question: Which one of the following statements regarding acne vulgaris is incorrect?
options: Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation results in obstruction of the pilosebaceous follicle
Acne vulgaris affects at least 80% of teenagers

A 24-year-old Greek woman attends an endocrinology clinic with facial hair that she finds embarrassing and upsetting.

Bloods tests show the following:


Testosterone	1.7 nmol/L	(0.2 - 1.7)
TSH	3.8mU/L	(0.27 - 4.2)
Free T4	18pmol/L	(12 - 22)
Prolactin	325	(<700)
Cortisol	422 nmol/L	(140 - 690)

Ultrasound abdomen: 7 immature follicles within the left ovary, 2 immature follicles within the right ovary, both ovaries normal volume. Normal appearance of other pelvic viscera.

Her periods are normal, her BMI is 20kg/m2, and she has one child aged 2.

She is keen to reduce the appearance of her facial hair.

What treatment would you recommend?
explanation:
Topical eflornithine is the treatment of choice for facial hirsutism

In around 20% of women with hirsutism, no cause is identified. Hirsutism is more common in those of Mediterranean or Middle Eastern descent.

Causes of hirsutism can include drugs (e.g. steroids, ciclosporin, danazol), polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), and androgen-secreting tumours.

PCOS is defined by the Rotterdam criteria and can be diagnosed if a patient meets two of the following:

Oligo or an-ovulation
Biochemical and or clinical signs of hyperandrogenism
Polycystic ovaries (i.e. More than or equal to 12 follicles in each ovary or raised ovarian volume)

The patient in the stem does not meet the Rotterdam criteria. Following the screening tests done, no specific cause has been found for her hirsutism.

Topical eflornithine

acts on the hair follicle to inhibit hair growth. It is the first-line treatment for facial hirsutism and results are usually seen after 6-8 weeks. Hair growth returns if the use of this treatment is stopped.

Combined oral contraceptive pill

is a second-line treatment for pre-menopausal hirsutism.

Electrolysis

is a method of hair reduction that destroys hair follicles. It is painful and impractical for larger areas. It could be an option, but topical eflornithine is recommended first-line.

Metformin

is used to improve hirsutism for PCOS patients. In this case, the patient does not have symptoms of PCOS - her periods are regular, testosterone levels are normal.

Cyproterone acetate

is an anti-androgen that is used to treat androgen-dependent conditions including excessive hair growth. It is not first-line in the treatment of facial hirsutism.

question:
A 47-year-old woman is seen in the Nephrology clinic as part of her follow-up for end-stage renal failure secondary to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. She has hypertension, for which she is taking ramipril, but is otherwise relatively well. As such, she is offered the option of a renal transplant.

What malignancy is she most likely to develop if she does proceed to transplantation?
options: Basal cell carcinoma of the skin
Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
correctText: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
explanation:
Renal transplant patients - skin cancer (particularly squamous cell) is the most common malignancy secondary to immunosuppression

The correct answer is

squamous cell carcinoma of the skin

. All patients who undergo a renal transplant are at an increased risk of a number of malignancies, due to T-cell ablating immunosuppression, which inhibits the immune system's normal ability to recognise and kill neoplastic cells. Of these, the most common cancer after a renal transplant is squamous cell skin cancer, which is approximately 250 times more common in renal transplant patients than in the general population.

Malignant melanoma

is incorrect. Although renal transplant patients have an increased likelihood of developing malignant melanoma compared to the general population, neither the incidence ratio nor the absolute probability of developing malignant melanoma is as high as for squamous cell skin cancer.

Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD)

is incorrect. PTLD tends to manifest as a non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in renal transplant recipients. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is around 5-15 times more common in this patient cohort than in the general population but is still not as common as squamous cell skin cancer.

Renal cell carcinoma

is a relatively rare complication of renal transplantation. Like most malignancies, its incidence is increased in renal transplant patients, but it is far less common than squamous cell skin cancer.

question: A 35-year-old man presents with an itchy, scaly rash that has gradually developed over the past few months. He is normally fit and well and the only past medical history of note is generalised anxiety disorder. On examination he has a number of ill-defined, pink coloured patches with a yellow/brown scale.The main affected areas are the sternum, eyebrows and the nasal bridge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
An itchy rash affecting the face and scalp distribution is commonly caused by seborrhoeic dermatitis

The distribution is very typical for seborrhoeic dermatitis. Atopic dermatitis presents more commonly in the flexural areas and does not have the same characteristic scale.

Pityriasis rosea typically presents with a herald patch (usually on trunk) followed by erythematous, oval, scaly patches which follow a characteristic distribution with the longitudinal diameters of the oval lesions running parallel to the line of Langer. This may produce a 'fir-tree' appearance.

question:
A 7-year-old child is admitted to hospital after presenting with a rapidly progressing, painful rash. The child was previously well. The child's only past medical history includes asthma and eczema. The patient's regular medications are a salbutamol inhaler with a spacer, and topical emollients. There is no significant family history. On examination, monomorphic punched-out erosions are noted by the doctor.

Which of the following is recognised as a common cause of this condition?
explanation:
Eczema herpeticum is a primary infection of the skin caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) and uncommonly coxsackievirus

The history and examination points towards a diagnosis of eczema herpeticum, which requires admission for treatment with intravenous aciclovir. The correct answer here is herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2. Less commonly, it can be caused by coxsackievirus A16.

Herpes simplex viruses 3 and 4 do not exist.

Human herpesviruses 3 and 4 are varicella-zoster virus and Epstein-Barr virus respectively. The former causes chickenpox, and the latter is implicated in several diseases, including infectious mononucleosis.

Human herpesviruses 6 and 8 are incorrect - the former is implicated in several diseases, including the childhood illness roseola infantum, and the latter causes Kaposi's sarcoma.

Human papillomaviruses 6 and 11 are incorrect - these are common causes of genital warts (unlike 16 and 18, which are strongly linked to cervical cancer).

question:
A 52-year-old female with a background of hepatitis C presents with a rash on her face and hands.

On examination, you note onycholysis and a blistering erythematous rash on the dorsal aspect of the hand, which is also present on the face. You also note hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis on the face.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hepatitis C may lead to porphyria cutanea tarda

This patient is presenting with typical external features of porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT): blisters, onycholysis, hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis. In her case, this is likely due to her hepatitis C status, although oestrogen is known to play a role in PCT.

Pemphigus vulgaris is a valid differential for any blistering skin condition. However, it is not the most likely diagnosis in a patient with known hepatitis C and the other typical signs of PCT.

Pompholyx (dyshidrotic) eczema typically presents on the inside of the fingers, palms, toes rather than the dorsum of the hand or the face. Again it can cause blisters (and is relatively common) and therefore is not an unreasonable guess without seeing a photo of the rash, but is not the most likely diagnosis in this scenario.

Primary biliary cirrhosis can cause itching and hyperpigmentation, typically over pressure areas, but would usually present with jaundice (particularly in an exam setting) and not with blisters.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is less likely as there is no history of inflammatory bowel disease. In 80% of the patients with PSC, and certainly in most of the exam cases, there is a background of ulcerative colitis (or much more rarely, of Crohn's disease or HIV). Again it would likely present with itching and jaundice, rather than blisters.

A 62-year-old woman presents to her GP with an itchy rash of several weeks' duration. She describes the rash as being present on her hands and around the elbows. She is otherwise well and has no past medical history except for hypertension.

On examination, a papular, polygonal, violaceous, flat-topped rash is present on the palms, in her elbow creases and on the soles of her feet.

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the first-line treatment?
explanation:
Potent topical steroids are the first-line treatment for lichen planus

The diagnosis here is that of lichen planus, given the history and examination findings. In the first instance, a potent topical steroid should be used - and so topical clobetasol is the correct answer. Weaker steroids, such as hydrocortisone, are often ineffective.

Oral acitretin is incorrect. This is a retinoid, a second-line alternative to oral steroids if topical steroids are not effective. However, this patient should try topical steroids first.

Oral azathioprine is incorrect - this is an immunosuppressant and comes with significant side effects of its own. This will be used in significant, refractory disease if other oral measures have failed.

Oral prednisolone is incorrect - this is a second-line option if topical steroids fail to control the rash.

Topical emollients are incorrect. Whilst useful in alleviating itch and general symptoms, they will not help to resolve the disease.

question:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the general practice by his mother, reporting a sudden onset of a rash on his arms, chest, and around his mouth. On examination, you observe multiple monomorphic papulovesicular lesions with punched-out erosions, each approximately 1-2mm in diameter, accompanied by crusting over the lesions.

The child has a history of eczema and recently commenced nursery school.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Eczema herperticum rash can be described as monomorphic punched-out erosions (circular, depressed, ulcerated lesions) usually 1-3 mm in diameter

The most likely diagnosis is

eczema herpeticum

. This condition is a severe primary infection of the skin by herpes simplex virus 1 or 2, often seen in children with atopic eczema. The child's presentation of monomorphic papulovesicular lesions with punched-out erosions, each approximately 1-2mm in diameter, accompanied by crusting over the lesions is consistent with this diagnosis. Additionally, the sudden onset of the rash and his history of eczema further support this diagnosis.

Erythema multiforme

is characterised by the appearance of target lesions on the palms and soles, which subsequently spread to the torso and limbs. This is not described in this case.

Impetigo

is recognised by its hallmark golden-crusted lesions, frequently located around the mouth. Although this case describes crusting, it is not golden, and the other features are more consistent with eczema herpeticum.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome

predominantly affects infants and presents with a severe desquamating rash that progresses to form superficial fluid-filled blisters. This is not described in this case.

Varicella zoster virus infection

(chickenpox) manifests initially as an erythematous maculopapular rash, which evolves into vesicles filled with clear fluid. This is not described in this case.

The patient has tried using an emollient and topical hydrocortisone with no result. On examination, you note a number of depigmented patches on the dorsum of both hands. A 52-year-old woman presents to her GP with a persistent rash. She describes it as being itchy and being on the palms and inside the elbow creases.

On examination, there are several violaceous, polygonal papules and plaques with some overlying white scale, on the palms and flexor surfaces of the arms. Close examination of the hands also reveals mild oncodystrophy.

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Potent topical steroids are the first-line treatment for lichen planus

The correct answer is topical betamethasone. The diagnosis here is that of lichen planus, given the clear description and distribution of the rash. The first-line treatment for this condition is potent topical steroids; patients may have already tried mild steroids over-the-counter, which will have been unsuccessful.

Oral acitretin is incorrect. This is a retinoid and may be used second-line, but potent steroids should be tried first. Acitretin also plays a role in the management of psoriasis.

Oral ciclosporin is incorrect. This is an immunomodulator and may be used third-line, once other options have failed. It would not be used first-line, given its extensive side effects.

Oral prednisolone is incorrect. As an oral steroid, this would be an alternative second-line option to acitretin. First, however, topical steroids should be tried, due to fewer systemic side effects than oral steroids.

Topical emollient is incorrect - whilst often useful in generally alleviating itchy symptoms of a rash, they will do nothing to actually control the lichen planus.

question: A 14-year-old male is reviewed due to a patch of scaling and hair loss on the right side of his head. A skin scraping is sent which confirms a diagnosis of tinea capitis. Which organism is most likely to be responsible?

A 28-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with an itchy rash on his buttocks. He has a past medical history of coeliac disease.

On examination, there is a vesicular rash on both buttocks.

What will a biopsy of the lesion demonstrate?
options: Deposition of IgA on the blood vessel wall
Deposition of IgG, IgM and C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction
IgM deposition along the basement membrane
Linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
explanation:
Dermatitis herpetiformis - caused by IgA deposition in the dermis

IgA deposition

in the dermis is correct. The patient has an itchy vesicular rash on the buttocks with a background of coeliac disease. This is highly likely to be dermatitis herpetiformis which is associated with coeliac disease. If biopsied, the lesions will demonstrate IgA deposition in the dermis on immunofluorescence.

Deposition of IgA on the blood vessel wall

is incorrect. This is the characteristic finding in IgA vasculitis, which can cause lesions on the buttocks. However, the lesions are vasculitic rather than vesicular and this disorder is also associated with other clinical findings like abdominal pain, arthritis, and renal involvement, which are absent in this case.

Deposition of IgG, IgM and C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction

is incorrect. This is the so-called 'lupus band' typical of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE). This type of rash is typically macular rather than vesicular.

IgM deposition along the basement membrane

is incorrect. This is typical of scleroderma. There is no suggestion in this case that there is any skin hardening or thickening and scleroderma is not typically associated with vesicular lesions.

Linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane

is incorrect. This is a typical biopsy finding in bullous pemphigoid, which is another blistering skin disorder. This condition is present is more likely to be widespread rather than just affecting the buttocks. The lesions are larger (i.e. vesicles versus bullae) and may affect the mucus membranes.

A 22-year-old woman presents with itchy blisters on her hands. She says the lesions first appeared on her fingers and then spread to her palms. She complains of intense pruritus resistant to over the counter ointments. She is an art student and recently got a summer job at a children's summer camp where she leads athletics and arts and crafts sessions.

On examination, there are tense vesicles on her fingers and the palms of her hands without erythema. Her past medical history is significant for asthma which is well-controlled with a salbutamol inhaler. She takes cetirizine daily during the summer months for hay fever.

Which of the following is most likely to precipitate this condition?
explanation:
Pompholyx eczema may be precipitated by humidity (e.g. sweating) and high temperatures

Pompholyx eczema (also known as dyshidrotic dermatitis) is a common condition characterised by an intensely pruritic vesicular eruption on the palms and soles.

Although the aetiology is unknown triggers include

humidity e.g. increased sweating (due to climate, hyperhidrosis)
irritants e.g. water, detergents, metals (nickel)
lifestyle e.g. smoking
drug use e.g. aspirin and COCP

question: A 34-year-old man with a history of polyarthralgia, back pain and diarrhoea is found to have a 3 cm red lesion on his shin which is starting to ulcerate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 42-year-old woman presents to the haematology clinic with a 6-month history of episodic flushing and abdominal pain. Examination reveals multiple brown macules on her trunk that develop wheals when rubbed. Blood film shows monocytosis.


Serum tryptase	28 ng/mL	(<11.4)

What is the most appropriate next investigation to establish a definitive diagnosis?
explanation:
Bone marrow biopsy is the gold-standard investigation used to diagnose systemic mastocytosis

Bone marrow biopsy

is the correct answer as it represents the gold-standard investigation for definitively diagnosing systemic mastocytosis. This patient presents with classic features including urticaria pigmentosa (brown macules that wheal when rubbed - Darier's sign), flushing, abdominal pain, monocytosis, and significantly elevated serum tryptase levels. While elevated tryptase (>20 ng/mL persistently) is a minor diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis, definitive diagnosis requires bone marrow examination. The biopsy allows for histological assessment of mast cell infiltration, immunohistochemistry to identify aberrant mast cell markers (such as CD25 and CD2), and molecular testing for the KIT D816V mutation, which is present in over 90% of cases. These findings form the major diagnostic criteria according to WHO classification.

24-hour urinary histamine

can be elevated in systemic mastocytosis and may support the diagnosis, but it is primarily used to monitor disease activity rather than establish the initial diagnosis. It is not specific for mastocytosis and can be elevated in other conditions causing mast cell degranulation.

Chromogranin A level

is a neuroendocrine marker that would be more relevant in investigating carcinoid syndrome, which can present with flushing but would not typically cause the skin lesions or monocytosis seen in this case.

CT chest, abdomen and pelvis

might identify organomegaly or lymphadenopathy associated with systemic mastocytosis, but imaging alone cannot provide the definitive diagnosis required for this condition.

Flow cytometry of peripheral blood

is not routinely used in diagnosing systemic mastocytosis as circulating mast cells are typically very low in number, even in systemic disease. The abnormal mast cells are predominantly found in tissue, particularly bone marrow.

question:
A 25-year-old swimmer with Cushing's syndrome presents with a mildly itchy rash on her trunk with the presence of multiple discrete light-brown patches associated with superficial scaling.

What is the most appropriate treatment for this rash?
explanation:
Ketoconazole shampoo is used to treat pityriasis versicolor

Pityriasis versicolor is a common yeast infection of the skin, in which flaky discoloured patches appear on the chest and back.

Ketoconazole or selenium sulphide shampoo are antifungal shampoos which are often the first treatment recommended for pityriasis versicolor.

Terbinafine cream along with clotrimazole cream and miconazole cream can also be used as topical antifungal agents to apply to the skin. These reduce the number of skin yeasts.

Hydrocortisone cream is not useful in pityriasis versicolor. Steroid creams can be helpful for some skin problems and can even temporarily reduce ringworm symptoms like itching and redness, but they don't kill the fungus. Steroid creams also can make conditions like ringworm worse because they weaken the skin's defences.

Vitamin D analogues such as calcipotriol and calcitriol help regulate the immune system in the skin and slow the overgrowth of skin that happens in psoriasis but are not useful in conditions like pityriasis versicolor.

Ketoconazole cream is indicated for the topical treatment of fungal conditions such as tinea corporis, tinea cruris and tinea pedis but not pityriasis versicolor.

question:
A 48-year-old female presents to the acute medical unit with diarrhoea. She is passing 8 loose stools per day with occasional blood. Her past medical history includes metastatic melanoma and hypercholesterolemia and she is on nivolumab and atorvastatin. She does not smoke or drink alcohol and lives with her husband and three children. Recently, she completed a three-day course of trimethoprim for an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection.

Her observations are heart rate 93 beats per minute, blood pressure 105/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air and temperature 37.4ºC.

On examination, there is moderate diffuse abdominal tenderness. Bowel sounds are present and her abdomen is soft with no abdominal rigidity.

Blood test results:



Hb	111 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	444 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	4.8 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	131 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.0 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	9.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	126 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	45 mg/L	(< 5)
Lactate	2.4 mmol/L	(0.5-2.2)

Plain radiography of the colon demonstrates the diameter of the transverse colon to be 4.9cm.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Immune related adverse events in a patient on checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. nivolumab)? Need to treat with corticosteroids

Infliximab is incorrect. The diagnosis is an immune-related adverse event (in this case colitis) secondary to treatment with a checkpoint inhibitor nivolumab. The first-line treatment in moderately severe cases such as this one is oral prednisolone at a dose of approximately 1mg/kg. If the patient is refractory to steroids then an anti-TNF biologic such as infliximab may be used.

Mesalazine is incorrect. This is not used to induce remission in moderate-severe colitis but has a place in the maintenance of remission in mild-moderate disease.

Oral vancomycin is incorrect. The antibiotic trimethoprim is not typically associated with the development of

Clostridium difficile

diarrhoea. The context of this scenario points towards an immune-related adverse event.

Surgery is incorrect. This woman's abdominal radiograph demonstrates a transverse colon diameter of < 6cm, indicating that she does not have toxic megacolon and therefore surgical intervention is not warranted. She should be managed medically in the first instance. Her lactate is only mildly elevated in the context of likely dehydration and acute kidney injury.

Oral prednisolone is correct. This woman presents with colitis-associated with nivolumab. She has moderately severe disease requiring hospital admission and treatment but does not require urgent surgical intervention or high dose intravenous steroids in the first instance. She should be treated with oral prednisolone and rehydrated before other options are considered.

question: A 63-year-old man who is known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a number of lesions over his shins. On examination there are a number of 3-4 mm smooth, firm, papules which are hyperpigmented and centrally depressed. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Which organism has been implicated in the aetiology of this condition?
explanation:
Herpes hominis virus 7 (HHV-7) is thought to play a role in the aetiology of pityriasis rosea

The answer is herpes hominis virus 7 (HHV-7). The other options are not associated with pityriasis rosea.

Parvovirus B-19 is associated with slapped cheek syndrome.

Coxsackie B virus is an enterovirus associated with Bornholm disease, pericarditis, myocarditis and aseptic meningitis.

Streptococcus pyogenes

is a Lancefield Group A streptococcus implicated in the parthenogenesis of scarlet fever.

Streptococcus agalactiae

is a Lancefield Group B streptococcus associated with neonatal meningitis.
