In contrast, the vast majority of patients with pemphigus vulgaris have mucosal lesions, and the mouth is the most common site of presentation. Tense bullae are rarely seen as blisters are flaccid and easily rupture (reflecting the fact that it is a disease affecting the epidermis), resulting in painful erosions.

Epidermolysis bullosa describes a group of rare genetic conditions that result in easy blistering of the skin and mucous membranes. It is invariably diagnosed at a much younger age.

Shingles presents as a vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution, rather than tense blisters.

question: A 17-year-old male is reviewed six weeks after starting an oral antibiotic for acne vulgaris. He stopped taking the drug two weeks ago due to perceived alteration in his skin colour, and denies been exposed to strong sunlight for the past six months. On examination he has generalised increased skin pigmentation, including around the buttocks. Which one of the following antibiotics was he likely to be taking?

A 58-year-old woman presents with facial redness. This has been worsening since her holiday to Spain but she is otherwise asymptomatic.

She has a background of hypertension and takes amlodipine 5mg OD. She has no allergies and has not started any new medications recently.

On examination, telangiectasia are present with papules and pustules clustered around her nose and cheeks. She is afebrile.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Rosacea features:

This is a typical example of acne rosacea, presenting as a pronounced facial rash in middle-age, which has worsened after recent exposure to sunlight on holiday. Telangiectasia are common, which later develop into papules and pustules on the nose, cheeks and forehead.

Acne vulgaris is a good differential, however, this usually presents with skin lesions in adolescence. While rosacea is usually limited to the face, acne vulgaris can additionally affect the neck, chest and back.

Drug reactions take various forms, including urticarial rashes or - at the more extreme end of the spectrum - Stevens-Johnson syndrome. There is however no indication of new a medication being started and cutaneous adverse reactions to calcium channel blockers are extremely rare.

Erysipelas is a superficial cellulitis caused by group A beta-haemolytic streptococci. It has a characteristic butterfly distribution on the cheeks with a sharp, raised border. The skin appears firm, bright red and swollen.

Systemic lupus erythematous similarly presents with a butterfly-shaped rash across the cheeks and bridge of the nose, which tends to have a purple hue. This is an important differential to consider but, without clues towards multi-system involvement, rosacea is the most likely diagnosis.

question:
A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency room with a blistering rash on the backs of her hands and face. She has recently returned from a family holiday in Egypt. She reports that her father has experienced similar rashes previously. A urine sample reveals elevated levels of uroporphyrins.

What is the defective enzyme associated with the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda is caused by an inherited defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase

The correct answer is a defect in

uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase

, leading to the presentation of porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT). Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase converts uroporphyrinogen III into coproporphyrinogen III, one of the many reactions in synthesizing heme.  The patient has a new blistering rash on sun-exposed areas of the body after a holiday to a country with a hot climate, implying photosensitivity. Given the familial history and raised urinary uroporphyrinogen the most likely diagnosis is PCT.

PCT classically presents with a photosensitive, fragile and blistering rash on the face and dorsal aspects of the hands. Hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation may also be present. Patients will have a raised uroporphyrinogen and pink fluorescence of the urine when viewed under Wood's lamp.

All of the options are involved in the biosynthesis of haem and are disrupted by other causes of pathologies:

ALA synthase

converts glycine and succinyl-CoA to delta-aminolevulinic acid. It is disrupted in X-linked sideroblastic anaemia.

Porphobilinogen deaminase

converts porphobilinogen into hydroxymethylbilane and is defective in acute intermittent porphyria.

Porphobilinogen synthase

is responsible for the conversion of delta-aminolevulinic acid into porphobilinogen and is disrupted in lead poisoning. It is also known as ALA dehydratase.

Protoporphyrin ferrochelatase

is responsible for the conversion of protoporphyrin into haem and is also defective in lead poisoning. It is implicated more in the development of erythropoietic protoporphyria.

question:
A 38-year-old man is referred to the dermatology outpatient department with a recurrent rash on his face and dorsal hands, which seems to be precipitated by occasional alcohol use and sun exposure. He has no past medical history.

On examination, a blistering rash was noted on his face and dorsal hands. Diffuse excessive hair growth is noted throughout his body.

Blood tests are performed.


Hb	136 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	189 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	4.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Hepatitis C antibodies	negative

What is the underlying mechanism that explains his symptoms?
options: Mutations in the gene that encodes Δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthetase
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda is caused by an inherited defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase

Inherited defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase

is correct. The patient presents with a blistering rash on the face and dorsal hands provoked by sunlight and alcohol. In addition, there is hypertrichosis (excessive hair growth in non-androgen-dependent areas of the body). These findings suggest a diagnosis of porphyria cutanea tarda. This can be inherited or acquired due to hepatocyte damage (i.e. hepatitis C infection or alcohol excess). In the setting of negative testing for hepatitis C and the absence of alcohol excess, this is likely due to an inherited defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Hepatitis C is a common cause of porphyria cutanea tarda and serology should always be checked in suspected cases.

Inhibition of Δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD)

is incorrect. This is another defect in the haem metabolism pathway and is the main mechanism by which lead poisoning causes iron deficiency. The patient is not anaemic and there is no suggestion of lead poisoning, which does not cause this type of blistering rash or hypertrichosis.

Mutations in porphobilinogen deaminase

is incorrect. This is another defect in the haem metabolism pathway, resulting in acute intermittent porphyria. Recurrent attacks of abdominal pain and neurological dysfunction including peripheral neuropathy and seizures characterise this. These features are not present here and so it is PCT rather than AIP that is the likely disorder.

Mutations in the gene that encodes Δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthetase

are incorrect. This is another defect in the haem metabolism pathway. This causes sideroblastic anaemia. This is a differential for microcytic anaemia. This patient is not anaemic and therefore this is not the diagnosis.

question:
A 29-year-old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant presents to the antenatal clinic with a worsening rash on her legs. She had initially noticed multiple small red rounded lumps on both her lower legs. The lesions initially measured 3cm in diameter and have been slowly growing in size over the past two weeks. The lesions now range between 6-9cm nodules on both her shins which were becoming painful. This is her second pregnancy and she denied experiencing a similar rash before.

What is the likely cause for the rash in this case?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum may be caused by pregnancy

Erythema nodosum is a condition that causes painful red bumps under the skin on the shins. It is one of the most common forms of panniculitis that causes inflammation of the subcutaneous fat under the skin. It can occur in pregnancy due to hormonal changes.

Erythema ab igne is a skin reaction caused by chronic exposure to infrared radiation in the form of heat and is not commonly seen as a direct result of pregnancy.

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is a relatively common skin disorder that can occur in women during pregnancy. It usually presents within the first pregnancy. It appears as an itchy, bumpy rash that starts in the stretch marks of the abdomen in the last 3 months of pregnancy then clears with delivery. This is unlikely to be the case here.

Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction usually triggered by infections, most commonly herpes simplex virus (HSV) and can be associated with pregnancy. However, it appears as target-like patches (dark circles with purple-grey centres) which are not described here.

Erythema gyratum repens is a rare paraneoplastic type of annular erythema with a distinctive figurate 'wood-grain' appearance. It has a strong association with malignancy.

question:
A 28-year-old man attends the dermatology clinic with a rash. On examination, you note an erythematous yellow scaly rash over his nasolabial fold, upper back and chest.

What is a common complication of this condition?
explanation:
Otitis externa and blepharitis are common complications of seborrhoeic dermatitis

Otitis externa

is correct. This is a classic case of seborrhoeic dermatitis. Otitis externa is a frequent complication of this skin disorder.

Conjunctivitis

is incorrect. It is blepharitis which is associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis. Conjunctivitis rarely occurs.

Nephrotic syndrome

is incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome can occur as a complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The malar rash of SLE typically occurs across the cheeks and nose but can include the forehead and chin. Importantly it spares the nasolabial folds in contrast to seborrhoeic dermatitis, making it a less likely diagnosis in this case.

Otitis media

is incorrect. It is otitis externa rather than media which is a common complication of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Rhinophyma

is incorrect. This is a complication of rosacea which presents with scattered papules, pustules and telangiectasia over the nose, cheeks and forehead.

question:
A 26-year-old lady presents to you distressed due to the presence of a rash over her thorax and abdomen for the last three weeks. On examination, you note numerous teardrop lesions on her body.

She has no known past medical history and denies exposure to any new irritants. She states that she is going to be married in 2 weeks and wants to know if there is anything that can be done to hasten the disappearance of her rash.

Which therapy could this lady be commenced on?

A 68-year-old female presents to her primary healthcare provider with the complaints of painful blisters on the gingival and buccal mucosa and skin that rupture easily and cause ulcers. The oral blisters started two months ago and the cutaneous lesions just a week ago. She has a history of hypertension, vitiligo and diabetes mellitus type 2. Examination of the oral cavity and the skin reveals scattered shallow ulcerations 8 mm to 1 cm in diameter. Biopsy of the lesions showed acantholysis. She has been started on corticosteroids.

Which of the following is the most likely aetiology of the condition in this patient?
explanation:
Antibodies against desmoglein 3 are seen in pemphigus vulgaris

The sign and symptoms along with biopsy findings in the scenario are suggestive of pemphigus vulgaris. Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disease caused by antibodies directed against desmoglein 3, a cadherin-type epithelial cell adhesion molecule.

Antibodies against desmoplakin I are seen in paraneoplastic pemphigus.

Antibodies against desmocollin 1 are found in subcorneal pustular dermatosis type of IgA pemphigus.

Antibodies against desmoplakin II are also seen in paraneoplastic pemphigus.

Antibodies against desmoglein 1 are formed in pemphigus variants such as pemphigus foliaceous, pemphigus erythematosus and fogo selvagem.

question:
A 78-year-old man asks you to look at a lesion on the right side of nose which has been getting slowly bigger over the past 2-3 months. On examination you observe a round, raised, flesh coloured lesion which is 3mm in diameter and has a central depression. The edges of the lesion appear rolled and contain some telangiectasia.

What is the single most likely diagnosis?

A patient presents with a firm smooth growth on their upper chest, following an insect bite. You suspect a keloid scar and refer to dermatology.

What demographic of patients have a higher susceptibility to this type of scar formation?
explanation:
Keloid scars - more common in young, black, male adults

The correct answer is

young black adults

.

This patient has keloid scar formation, which is excessive scar formation usually occurring following skin injury, and which extends beyond the original wound margin. Keloid scars are more common in

young black adults.

In a study, as many as 16% of black individuals reported keloid scar formation.

Those with highly pigmented skin are 15 times more likely to develop keloid scars than those with less pigmented skin. Incidence is higher during puberty and pregnancy. While they can occur anywhere on the body, certain areas are more prone, such as the upper chest, shoulders, neck and ears.

Keloid scar development is rare at the extremes of age. They rarely occur in the

elderly

, in

young children

and are less common in

caucasian

patients.

question:
A 33-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with excessive hair growth on her face. She has a past medical history of obesity and her body mass index is 35 kg/m².

On examination, she has thick dark hair on her face.

After trialling weight loss, what pharmacological treatment is most appropriate?
explanation:
Topical eflornithine is the treatment of choice for facial hirsutism

Eflornithine

is the correct answer. The patient has thick dark hair on her face, which is consistent with facial hirsutism. It is likely that obesity is the cause in this case. Topical eflornithine is a treatment for facial hirsutism and when applied to the skin works by blocking the action of an enzyme in hair follicles that causes hair growth.

Corticosteroids

is incorrect. This condition would both worsen her obesity and may actually cause rather than treat hirsutism.

Diazoxide

is incorrect. This is used in the management of hypoglycaemia in those patients who use too much insulin. Rather than treating hirsutism, it causes hypertrichosis (which is androgen-independent hair growth).

Metformin

is incorrect. This may be effective in treating hirsutism in patients with polycystic ovary syndrome, which is not present in this case. In those patients with hirsutism limited to the face, topical eflornithine is a more appropriate choice.

Minoxidil

is incorrect. This is actually used to stimulate hair growth in men and women with hair loss.

question:
A 46-year-old man is being investigated for recurrent episodes of melaena. He gives a history of nosebleeds, which occur frequently, almost every week. He is not aware of his family history, as he was adopted.

Physical examination reveals telangiectasias over the lips and buccal mucosa. His blood tests are as follows:


Hb	90 g/L	(135 - 180)
Platelets	250 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.0 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Ferritin	5 ng/mL	(20 - 230)
Reticulocytes	0.3 %	(0.5 - 1.5)
Peripheral blood film	Microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes	

What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
explanation:
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia - autosomal dominant

The correct answer is

autosomal dominant

. The patient's symptoms suggest a diagnosis of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, which is an autosomal dominant condition. This means that an affected individual has a 50% chance of passing the disorder to each of their offspring. HHT is characterized by multiple telangiectasias over the skin and mucous membranes, frequent nosebleeds (epistaxis), and visceral lesions such as gastrointestinal telangiectasias which can cause bleeding and result in iron deficiency anaemia, as seen in this patient. Despite being adopted and unaware of his family history, the combination of his symptoms strongly suggests HHT.

Autosomal recessive

is incorrect. Some bleeding disorders with an autosomal recessive inheritance include platelet function disorders like Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard-Soulier syndrome, and patients will generally exhibit petechiae or ecchymoses on examination.

Mitochondrial inheritance

is incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance is a non-Mendelian type of inheritance where the transmission is entirely through the maternal line. All the offspring of an affected mother will be affected, whereas the offspring of an affected father do not inherit the disease. Mitochondrial disorders mainly have neurological manifestations, and examples include MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke) and Leber optic atrophy.

X-linked dominant

is incorrect. These conditions are very rare and can be remembered using the mnemonic FAIR COX, where F - Fragile X syndrome, A - Alport's syndrome, I - Incontinentia pigmenti, R - Retts syndrome, C - Charcot Marie Tooth disease type X, O - Orofaciodigital syndrome, X- X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets.

X-linked recessive

is incorrect. Bleeding disorders inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern include haemophilia A (due to factor VIII deficiency) and B (due to factor IX deficiency). These patients commonly have a history of ecchymoses and hematoma formation in their joints and soft tissues.

question: A 26-year-old man who is HIV positive is noted to have developed seborrhoeic dermatitis. Which of the following two complications are most associated with this condition?
explanation:
Otitis externa and blepharitis are common complications of seborrhoeic dermatitis

Alopecia is not commonly seen in seborrhoeic dermatitis, but may develop if a severe secondary infection develops

question:
A 28-year-old woman, currently 14 weeks pregnant, presents to her GP with worsening acne.

On examination, she has widespread non-inflammatory lesions, numerous papules and pustules, and extensive inflammatory lesions, some of which are nodules. She is concerned about the potential for pitting and scarring.

What medication should be commenced alongside topical benzoyl peroxide?
explanation:
Acne vulgaris in pregnancy - use oral erythromycin if treatment needed

Oral erythromycin

is the correct choice for this patient presenting with features in keeping with moderate to severe acne vulgaris. Erythromycin is a safe antibiotic option that effectively reduces bacterial proliferation and inflammation in acne. Given the patient is pregnant erythromycin is preferred because it does not pose significant risks to the developing foetus, unlike other medications such as isotretinoin or tetracyclines. Thus, combining oral erythromycin with topical benzoyl peroxide provides a suitable treatment approach for her acne while prioritising maternal and foetal safety.

Oral isotretinoin

is incorrect in this case because it is highly teratogenic and poses significant risks to a developing foetus, particularly in the first trimester. Its use is contraindicated in pregnancy due to the potential for severe birth defects and other complications.

Oral minocycline

is incorrect as it belongs to the tetracycline class of antibiotics, which is contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of adverse effects on the foetus. Tetracyclines can cause teeth discolouration and affect bone growth in the developing baby. Given that the patient is 14 weeks pregnant and experiencing moderate to severe acne, oral erythromycin is a safer option to manage her condition effectively while minimising risks to the foetus.

Topical dapsone

is incorrect for this case because, while it is generally considered safe for use during pregnancy, it is less effective for treating moderate to severe acne compared to other available options. Dapsone primarily targets inflammatory lesions but may not adequately address the widespread non-inflammatory lesions and papules described in this patient. Additionally, its efficacy in pregnancy has not been as well established as that of oral erythromycin, making it a less suitable choice for this situation.

Topical tazarotene

is incorrect because it is a potent retinoid that is contraindicated during pregnancy due to its potential teratogenic effects. The use of tazarotene can lead to serious risks for the developing foetus, including birth defects. Although it is effective for treating acne vulgaris by promoting cell turnover and reducing lesions, its safety profile makes it unsuitable for pregnant women, highlighting the need for safer alternatives like oral erythromycin in this context.

question: Which of the following skin conditions associated with malignancy are not correctly paired?
explanation:
Erythema gyratum repens is a paraneoplastic eruption with a 'wood-grain' pattern and figurate erythema commonly seen in patients with lung cancer

Erythema gyratum repens is generally associated with solid organ malignancies such as lung and breast cancer

question:
A 52-year-old woman presents with discomfort when eating. On examination, buccal white-lace pattern lesions and ulcers are seen in the mouth.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Oral lichen planus typically presents with buccal white-lace pattern lesions and ulcers

Oral lichen planus

classically produces a reticular, white-lacy network of Wickham’s striae on the buccal mucosa, exactly as described in this stem. The lesion represents a chronic T-cell-mediated inflammatory disorder affecting stratified squamous epithelium. Patients may report pain on eating spicy or acidic foods and, on examination, peripheral ulceration can accompany the white pattern. Recognition is important: in UK practice topical potent corticosteroids and benzydamine mouthwash offer symptomatic relief, while persistent cases require biopsy to exclude malignant transformation.

Behçet's disease

can certainly cause painful oral ulcers, but they are typically multiple, round or oval aphthous-like erosions without the fine white lacing. Genital ulceration, uveitis and a vasculitic rash elsewhere are usual accompaniments; their absence, coupled with the very specific mucosal appearance described, makes Behçet’s far less likely here.

Sjogren's syndrome

produces xerostomia and consequent oral soreness; secondary candidiasis or dental caries are common sequelae. However, it does not create a patterned white network on the mucosa. Examination generally reveals a dry, sticky oral cavity rather than discrete lace-like lesions, so the clinical picture does not fit.

Plaque psoriasis

can occasionally involve the oral cavity, but when it does the lesions are usually erythematous patches with a migratory quality (geographic tongue) or generalised erythema rather than reticular white striae. Furthermore, psoriatic skin plaques elsewhere on extensor surfaces would be expected in the majority of cases.

Oral candidiasis

is a tempting choice because it produces white patches in the mouth and can be uncomfortable when eating. Crucially, however, candidal plaques are creamy, can often be wiped off to leave an erythematous base and have no lace-like architecture. The description of a patterned white network and associated ulceration points firmly away from thrush and towards lichen planus.

question: A 60-year-old man is admitted to hospital with acute pneumonia. He has a past medical history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, alcohol excess and hypertension, and has been homeless for the last 12 years. On the post-take ward round, you notice that he has a brown-red discolouration of his face, neck, forearms and lower legs, with scaling and cracking of the skin. He complains that he is struggling to eat and drink and has persistent vomiting and diarrhoea. He seems a little disorientated. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely to be causing these symptoms?
explanation:
Deficiency of niacin (B3) causes pellagra

The correct answer is B3- niacin. The patient has some of the symptoms of pellagra, which is classically characterised by the triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. The 'dementia' more commonly presents subtly with low mood, irritability, apathy and anxiety, progressing to delusions, psychosis, drowsiness and coma.

DermNet NZ:

https://www.dermnetnz.org/topics/pellagra/

question:
A 29-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 0, presents to the fertility clinic. All 4 of her pregnancies resulted in spontaneous abortion after the 10th week of pregnancy. She also describes joint pain, discolouration of the fingers of both hands in cold weather and macular rashes.

The patient is sexually active and taking a daily prenatal multivitamin.

There is bilateral polyarthropathy with effusion affecting fingers, toes, and knees. There's an ulcer on the left middle finger. You also note alopecia and purple reticular rash on both calves.

What is the most specific test for the underlying condition?
explanation:
Livedo reticularis can be caused by SLE

The presentation of unexpected pregnancy loss fits best with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLS). In addition, the patient's symptoms of joint pain, Raynaud phenomenon, alopecia and livedo reticularis (purple reticular rash) point toward the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The presence of an ulcer over the finger suggests secondary vasculitis due to SLE. In this scenario, SLE is the underlying disease, for which the most sensitive test is an antinuclear antibody (ANA) with 100% sensitivity. However, there are other tests for SLE with better specificity. The most specific tests are anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) antibody and an

anti-Smith (Sm) antibody

with 99% specificity.

Anti-centromere antibodies

are strongly associated with CREST syndrome (calcinosis cutis, Raynaud phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia). Skin involvement is a defining feature of CREST syndrome, and includes thickening and hardening with redness and oedematous swelling. This is not provided with this patient.

Anti-histone antibodies

are present in more than 95% of patients with drug-induced lupus, especially among those taking procainamide, hydralazine, chlorpromazine, and quinidine. There is no such drug history in this patient.

Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies

are associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MP), and other autoimmune vasculitides. Though GPA and MP can lead to cutaneous ulceration, lack of upper respiratory tract (such as sinusitis), lower respiratory tract and renal involvement make them unlikely.

Due to its high sensitivity,

anti-nuclear antibodies

are present virtually in all patients with SLE. But it is a nonspecific marker as this is associated with several rheumatological autoimmune conditions.

question:
A 39-year-old female presents with well-demarcated red, scaly patches affecting the back of her elbows. These are making it hard to care for her newborn.

She has been taking paracetamol regularly since her cesarean section 1 month ago and is not breastfeeding.

At a medical review two weeks ago, she had been started on propranolol as required for anxiety, promethazine as required for insomnia, and a course of prednisolone for Bell's palsy.

Which of the following is most likely to have precipitated her symptoms?
explanation:
Beta-blockers are known to exacerbate plaque psoriasis

This patient is presenting with typical features of plaque psoriasis, i.e. well-demarcated, scaly, erythematous patches affecting the extensor surfaces - in this case, the back of her elbows.

Propranolol is a beta-blocker and these are known to exacerbate plaque psoriasis. The inflammatory effects occur primarily with fat-soluble beta-blockers, such as propranolol, as opposed to water-soluble ones, such as atenolol.

Psoriasis often improves during pregnancy. This is thought to be due to the rise in progesterone dampening the overactive immune response that triggers psoriasis. Indeed, psoriasis may flare up after delivery due to a fall in progesterone. Therefore, stating that a progesterone rise has caused the flare would be incorrect.

Prednisolone is often used as part of the treatment for psoriasis and would be very unlikely to exacerbate it.

Paracetamol, unlike aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, is not known to exacerbate psoriasis.

Promethazine is an antihistamine used for allergies, nausea and insomnia. It is not known to exacerbate psoriasis.

question: A 21-year-old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant present with worsening acne which she is finding distressing. She is currently using topical benzyl peroxide with limited effect. On examination there is widespread non-inflammatory lesions and pustules on her face. What is the most appropriate next management step?
explanation:
Acne vulgaris in pregnancy - use oral erythromycin if treatment needed

The correct answer is

Oral erythromycin

. According to the British National Formulary (BNF) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, oral erythromycin is considered safe for use in pregnancy if topical treatments are ineffective. It's a macrolide antibiotic that has anti-inflammatory properties which can help reduce acne lesions.

Oral trimethoprim

is not recommended in pregnancy due to its potential teratogenic effects. Trimethoprim acts as a folate antagonist, which could potentially lead to neural tube defects in the unborn child. It should be avoided especially during the first trimester of pregnancy when organogenesis takes place.

Oral lymecycline

and

Oral doxycycline

, both tetracycline antibiotics, are contraindicated in pregnancy. They are known to deposit in developing bones and teeth, leading to staining and enamel hypoplasia in children exposed in utero. They may also inhibit bone growth.

Finally,

Topical retinoid

is not recommended during pregnancy or for women planning a pregnancy due to its teratogenic risk. Retinoids are derivatives of vitamin A and have been associated with birth defects when used systemically. Whilst there isn't definitive evidence that topical retinoids pose the same risk, caution is advised due to systemic absorption potential.

question: Pellagra is caused by a deficiency in:
explanation:
Deficiency of niacin (B3) causes pellagra

Nicotinic acid

(vitamin B3) deficiency is indeed the cause of pellagra. This condition is characterised by the classic triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea, and dementia, sometimes with a fourth 'D' - death - if left untreated. The dermatitis typically affects sun-exposed areas, creating a distinctive photosensitive rash with a clear demarcation between affected and unaffected skin. Gastrointestinal symptoms include diarrhoea, vomiting, and inflammation of the mucous membranes. Neurological manifestations range from irritability and insomnia to confusion, memory loss, and psychosis. Nicotinic acid (niacin) is essential for the formation of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP), which are crucial for cellular metabolism, particularly in oxidation-reduction reactions. Pellagra is now rare in developed countries but may still occur in populations with maize-based diets (as maize contains niacin in a bound, non-bioavailable form), chronic alcoholism, malabsorption syndromes, or certain medications that interfere with niacin metabolism.

Vitamin B12

(cobalamin) deficiency does not cause pellagra. Instead, it leads to megaloblastic anaemia and neurological complications including peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, and cognitive impairment. B12 deficiency is commonly associated with pernicious anaemia (due to intrinsic factor deficiency), gastrectomy, ileal disease or resection, and strict vegan diets. The neurological symptoms of B12 deficiency can include paraesthesia, ataxia, and impaired position and vibration sense, which are distinct from the dementia seen in pellagra.

Thiamine

(vitamin B1) deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi. Wernicke's encephalopathy presents with the classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia, while Korsakoff's psychosis involves severe anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation. Beriberi can manifest as either 'dry' (neurological symptoms) or 'wet' (cardiovascular symptoms including high-output cardiac failure). Thiamine deficiency is commonly associated with chronic alcoholism, malabsorption, prolonged vomiting, or starvation. Unlike pellagra, thiamine deficiency does not typically cause the characteristic dermatitis.

Vitamin B2

(riboflavin) deficiency causes ariboflavinosis, which presents with angular stomatitis (cracks at the corners of the mouth), cheilosis (swollen, red lips), glossitis (magenta tongue), seborrhoeic dermatitis, and normocytic anaemia. While there is some overlap with the dermatological manifestations of pellagra, riboflavin deficiency does not cause the characteristic diarrhoea or dementia seen in pellagra. Riboflavin is a component of the flavin coenzymes FAD and FMN, which are important in oxidation-reduction reactions.

Vitamin B6

(pyridoxine) deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy, seborrhoeic dermatitis, glossitis, angular cheilitis, and, in severe cases, seizures. It may also lead to microcytic anaemia that is unresponsive to iron supplementation. Pyridoxine deficiency can occur due to certain medications (e.g., isoniazid, hydralazine), alcoholism, or malabsorption syndromes. While some skin manifestations may overlap with pellagra, the characteristic triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea, and dementia is not seen in vitamin B6 deficiency.

question:
A 29-year-old woman presents to her GP with several painful, red, raised lesions on her shins. She has also noted a thin, white, odourless vaginal discharge.

Over the last week, she has suffered from feeling increasingly nauseous. She has also been passing urine more frequently but denies dysuria/haematuria.

What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Urine sample for microscopy, culture and sensitivity
explanation:
Erythema nodosum may be caused by pregnancy

Pregnancy test

is correct. This patient has erythema nodosum, and the other symptoms she describes (non-offensive vaginal discharge, nausea and urinary frequency) are all physiological changes that occur during pregnancy. A pregnancy test is therefore the most appropriate next investigation.

Biopsy of the skin lesions

is incorrect. The features described are compatible with erythema nodosum accompanied by normal physiological changes of pregnancy. Erythema nodosum caused by pregnancy is self-limiting and is not known to cause any adverse outcomes for the mother or the baby. A biopsy is therefore unnecessarily invasive and would not change management.

High vaginal swab

is incorrect. A high vaginal swab can be used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis,

Trichomonas vaginalis

and

Candida

. Bacterial vaginosis is associated with a fishy discharge,

Trichomonas vaginalis

with a thin offensive smelling discharge and

Candida

with a white curd-like discharge. None of these fit the discharge described, and infections with these organisms would not explain the other symptoms she describes, which are all normal physiological changes associated with pregnancy.

Sputum sample for Ziehl-Neelsen staining

is incorrect. This is the test for mycobacteria such as

Mycobacterium tuberculosis

, but there are no strong indications that this patient has tuberculosis from the question stem, as the symptoms she describes suggest erythema nodosum accompanied by normal physiological changes of pregnancy.

Urine sample for microscopy, culture and sensitivity

is incorrect. This would provide evidence for urinary tract infection, amongst other things. This patient does note urinary frequency; however, a urinary tract infection would not explain the erythema nodosum or the vaginal discharge. These features can all be caused by pregnancy.

question: A 26-year-old man with a history of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia is planning to start a family. What is the mode of inheritance?
explanation:
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia - autosomal dominant

The correct answer is

Autosomal dominant

. Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, is a genetic disorder that follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. This means that an affected individual has a 50% chance of passing the condition to each of their offspring, regardless of sex. HHT is caused by mutations in several genes, most commonly ENG (endoglin), ACVRL1 (ALK1), or SMAD4, which are involved in the TGF-β signalling pathway that regulates blood vessel development and repair.

Autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance

is incorrect. While HHT does follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, it typically shows complete penetrance, meaning that virtually all individuals who inherit the mutation will develop some manifestations of the disease by adulthood. However, the severity and specific manifestations can vary widely between affected individuals, which is referred to as variable expressivity rather than incomplete penetrance.

Autosomal codominant

is incorrect. Codominance refers to a pattern where both alleles in a heterozygous individual are fully expressed, resulting in a phenotype that is a mixture of the two homozygous phenotypes. This is not the case with HHT, where a single mutated copy of the gene is sufficient to cause the disease, and there is no distinct phenotype associated with having two mutated copies (which is often lethal in embryonic development).

Autosomal recessive with incomplete penetrance

is incorrect on two counts. HHT is not an autosomal recessive condition, which would require two copies of the mutated gene to manifest the disease. Additionally, as mentioned earlier, HHT shows complete penetrance rather than incomplete penetrance.

Autosomal recessive

is incorrect. In autosomal recessive conditions, an individual must inherit two copies of the mutated gene (one from each parent) to develop the disease. Carriers with only one copy typically do not show symptoms. This is not the case with HHT, where a single copy of the mutated gene is sufficient to cause the disease, consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

Understanding the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern of HHT is crucial for providing appropriate genetic counselling to this patient who is planning to start a family, as each of his children will have a 50% chance of inheriting the condition.

question: A 26-year-old female, of Han Chinese origin, with newly diagnosed partial epilepsy is commenced on carbamazepine and has an HLA B*1502. Two weeks later, she develops a maculopapular rash, purpuric macules and targetoid lesions; full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and mucous membrane involvement.. What is the predominant cell type involved in this reaction?

A 23-year-old man presents as he is concerned over recent hair loss. Examination reveals a discrete area of hair loss on the left temporal region with no obvious abnormality of the underlying scalp. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 24-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a recurrent rash, which is often provoked by cold weather. She has no past medical history and does not take any regular medications.

On examination, there is a net-like pattern of reddish-blue skin discolouration that is non-blanching affecting her legs.

What condition is commonly associated with this type of rash?
explanation:
Livedo reticularis can be caused by SLE

Systemic lupus erythematosus

is correct. The description of a rash i.e. a net-like pattern of reddish-blue skin discolouration that is non-blanching is suggestive of livedo reticularis (LR). LR results from disturbed blood flow to the skin resulting in low blood flow and reduced oxygen tension at the skin surface. This results in higher amounts of deoxygenated haemoglobin resulting in subsequent discolouration. Postulated mechanisms in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) relate to microvascular thrombosis (in cases of an associated antiphospholipid syndrome), vasculitis and altered vascular tone. LR is associated with many other infective, inflammatory, haematological and malignant conditions.

Measles

is incorrect. LR is not associated with measles. The pathognomonic rash in measles is 'Koplik spots', white spots on the buccal mucosa with a blue-white centre and surrounding erythema.

Rheumatic fever

is incorrect. LR is not a feature of rheumatic fever. The cardinal rash in rheumatic fever is erythema marginatum described as a distinct type of annular erythema. The rash appears as red macules that spread outwards in a circular shape. As the lesions advance the edges elevate and become erythematous while the centre clears, giving the characteristic appearance.

Sarcoidosis

is incorrect. There is a diverse range of cutaneous manifestations of sarcoidosis including erythema nodosum (violaceous tender nodules) and lupus pernio (violaceous indurated plaques on the central face) but LR is not a feature of sarcoidosis, unlike many other inflammatory conditions.

Still's disease

is incorrect. A transient rash can be associated with Still's disease. However, it tends to be erythematous and blotchy and occurs typically on the chest rather than the legs. It is not provoked by cold and does not have a 'net-like' pattern.

question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the antenatal clinic at 34 weeks gestation with a 3-day history of an intensely pruritic rash. It started around her abdominal striae and has spread to her thighs. On examination, she has erythematous papules and plaques with excoriations. There are no vesicles or bullae. She is otherwise well with normal vital signs.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is not associated with blistering

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy

is the most likely diagnosis in this case. This pruritic condition typically presents in the third trimester of pregnancy, with lesions often first appearing in the abdominal striae before spreading to other areas such as the thighs. The characteristic features include intensely pruritic erythematous papules and plaques without blistering. The absence of vesicles or bullae is a key distinguishing feature. Management includes emollients, mild potency topical steroids, and in severe cases, oral steroids. The condition is benign and self-limiting, typically resolving within weeks after delivery without any adverse effects on the mother or baby.

Atopic eruption of pregnancy

is the most common skin disorder in pregnancy, but it typically presents as an eczematous, itchy red rash. While it can occur at any stage of pregnancy, it often appears earlier than polymorphic eruption of pregnancy. The distribution is typically on the flexural surfaces rather than starting in the abdominal striae. The patient's presentation with papules and plaques starting in the abdominal striae is more consistent with polymorphic eruption of pregnancy.

Herpes gestationis

is an outdated term for pemphigoid gestationis, which is characterized by pruritic blistering lesions. The absence of vesicles or bullae in this patient makes this diagnosis unlikely. Herpes gestationis/pemphigoid gestationis is an autoimmune blistering disease that can recur in subsequent pregnancies and is associated with increased fetal risks.

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

presents with generalized pruritus without a primary skin rash. The pruritus typically affects the palms and soles and is associated with elevated bile acids and liver enzymes. The presence of a visible rash with papules and plaques in this patient makes intrahepatic cholestasis unlikely.

Pemphigoid gestationis

is characterized by pruritic blistering lesions that often develop in the peri-umbilical region before spreading. The hallmark of this condition is the presence of vesicles and bullae, which are absent in this patient. Pemphigoid gestationis is an autoimmune blistering disorder that requires oral corticosteroids for management and can be associated with adverse fetal outcomes.

question: A 9-year-old child with a history of atopic eczema presents with a sudden worsening of her skin. Her eczema is usually well controlled with emollients but her parents are concerned as the facial eczema has got significantly worse overnight. She now has painful clustered blisters on both cheeks, around her mouth on her neck. Her temperature is 37.9ºC. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Eczema herpeticum is a serious condition that requires IV antivirals

The correct answer is

intravenous aciclovir

. This case describes eczema herpeticum (Kaposi's varicelliform eruption), which is a widespread herpes simplex virus infection occurring in patients with pre-existing skin conditions, most commonly atopic eczema. The presentation of clustered painful blisters, fever, and sudden worsening in a child with atopic eczema is characteristic. This is a medical emergency requiring prompt treatment with systemic antiviral therapy to prevent complications such as disseminated infection, keratoconjunctivitis, and potential mortality.

Advise paracetamol + emollients and reassure

would be inadequate management for eczema herpeticum. While these measures may provide symptomatic relief, they do not address the underlying viral infection which requires specific antiviral treatment.

Potent topical steroid

would be contraindicated in this situation. Using topical steroids in the presence of active viral infection could worsen the condition by suppressing local immune responses and allowing the infection to spread.

Intravenous flucloxacillin

would not be appropriate as first-line treatment. While secondary bacterial infection can occur, the primary problem is viral and requires antiviral therapy. Antibiotics may be added if there is evidence of bacterial superinfection.

Oral fluconazole

would not be appropriate as this is an antifungal medication. The presentation is not consistent with a fungal infection, and antifungal therapy would not address the underlying viral cause of eczema herpeticum.

question:
A 24-year-old woman with a background of acne vulgaris has been referred to the clinic due to a flare of her acne causing scarring and hyperpigmentation. She is 14 weeks pregnant with her first child and thinks this may have triggered the flare. She has used tretinoin and doxycycline to manage her skin successfully in the past but changed to her current regime of topical benzoyl peroxide with topical clindamycin 6 months ago as she wanted to conceive.

What is the most appropriate treatment option in this case?
options: Continue topical benzoyl peroxide, change topical clindamycin to oral erythromycin
Continue topical clindamycin, stop benzoyl peroxide and add doxycycline
Continue topical clindamycin, stop benzoyl peroxide and restart topical tretinoin
Stop current treatment, start oral erythromycin alone
correctText: Continue topical benzoyl peroxide, change topical clindamycin to oral erythromycin
explanation:
Acne vulgaris in pregnancy - use oral erythromycin if treatment needed

The most appropriate course of action would be to

continue topical benzoyl peroxide and change topical clindamycin to oral erythromycin

. The severity of the case is demonstrated by the presence of nodules and resultant scarring, necessitating an escalation in treatment. Erythromycin represents a safe alternative to tetracyclines during pregnancy, and the continued use of benzoyl peroxide is advised as it helps reduce the risk of developing antibiotic resistance. According to NICE guidelines, there are multiple first-line treatment options available; however, this combination is the only suitable option for this patient that avoids retinol or tetracycline, both of which are contraindicated during pregnancy.

It would not be ideal to

continue the current treatment

. The development of scarring and hyperpigmentation would warrant treatment escalation by switching to an oral antibiotic or considering introducing a retinol if not contraindicated as in this case. Switching to oral erythromycin and continuing topical benzoyl peroxide is the preferred option.

It would be inappropriate to

continue topical clindamycin, stop benzoyl peroxide and add doxycycline

. NICE guidelines specifically recommend against using both oral and topical antibiotics concurrently due to concerns over increasing antibiotic resistance. Additionally, doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.

To

continue topical clindamycin, stop benzoyl peroxide and restart topical tretinoin

could be considered a reasonable approach for patients who are not pregnant; however, tretinoin is contraindicated in this case. Both topical and oral retinoids must be avoided during pregnancy.

Finally, it would be inappropriate to

stop the current treatment and start oral erythromycin alone

, as monotherapy with antibiotics is discouraged by NICE guidance in the management of acne due to the increased risk of resistance. Instead, adjunctive use of benzoyl peroxide with antibiotics is recommended for its role in preventing antibiotic resistance.

question:
A 62-year-old Caucasian man is seen in the dermatology clinic with a 2-week history of a rapidly evolving itchy rash. The rash predominantly affects his under arms and has since spread to the palms of his hands and soles of his feet. He has a past medical history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) for which he takes regular inhaled Trimbow (beclometasone dipropionate, formoterol fumarate and glycopyrronium bromide) and salbutamol as required. He has no allergies and denies using new creams or detergents on his skin.

On examination, his observations are recorded within the normal range. He has thickened patches of skin in his axillae and on his palms and soles. The skin is discoloured and appears as a light-brown colour. Multiple excoriations and skin tags are seen surrounding the lesions. He has conjunctival pallor and there are small finger-like projections protruding from his lips but there is no other mucosal involvement.

What is the most important investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
The most common malignancy associated with acanthosis nigricans

This patient has acanthosis nigricans, a dermatological condition characterised by darker and thickened lesions typically involving the axilla, groin and back of the neck. Given this patient's age and the rapid onset of his presentation, it is likely that this patient has malignant acanthosis nigricans. Symptoms of pruritis and the presence of more extensive lesions involving the palms, soles and mucosa is more typical of malignant acanthosis nigricans. The most common underlying malignancy associated with this condition is gastric cancer. Risk factors for gastric adenocarcinoma include smoking and male sex. Along with computed tomography (CT) imaging, a gastroduodenoscopy would be indicated to investigate for a gastric malignancy.

Acanthosis nigricans is associated with multiple underlying conditions with one common condition being diabetes mellitus. Therefore, it is important to measure this patient's fasting blood glucose. However, diabetes is less likely to cause such severe symptoms compared to malignancy. Therefore, although it is a necessary investigation to complete, it will not confirm this patient's underlying diagnosis.

A chest x-ray would be appropriate if an underlying lung malignancy was expected. Whilst it should be considered in a patient with appearances suggestive of malignancy and a background of COPD, the most common malignancy associated with acanthosis nigricans is gastric adenocarcinoma.

A synacthen test is used to diagnose Addison's disease. Secondary to excess ACTH acting on melanocytes, patients with Addison's disease may have patches of hyperpigmented skin. However, the pattern of skin involvement is different to acanthosis nigricans and it would not explain this patient's pruritis or papilliform mucosal involvement, making it a less suitable choice.

A skin biopsy can be taken in patients with acanthosis nigricans if there is no clear underlying cause. It is also a useful diagnostic test to rule out other dermatological conditions, particularly those also associated with malignancy such as dermatomyositis. However, this patient's presentation points toward an underlying malignancy for which the most appropriate investigation out the options given would be a gastroduodenoscopy.

question:
A 25-year-old woman presents to her GP with scaly, discoloured patches on her chest and back. She reports that these patches become more pronounced after sun exposure and are accompanied by mild itching. Physical examination reveals multiple hypopigmented, well-demarcated patches with fine scaling.

What is the most appropriate treatment option for this patient?
explanation:
Ketoconazole shampoo is used to treat pityriasis versicolor

The description of the rash is consistent with pityriasis versicolor (also known as tinea versicolor). It is a fungal infection of the skin (caused by Malassezia) that is localised to the outermost layer of the epidermis. It is characterised by scaly, discoloured patches that do not tan in the sun and may cause mild itching. Risk factors for this condition include hyperhidrosis, malnutrition, immunodeficiency and being in a warm, humid environment.

Ketoconazole shampoo

is the first-line treatment for pityriasis versicolor as it targets the Malassezia yeast responsible for the condition. It is usually applied once daily for up to 5 days.

Hydrocortisone cream

is a low-potency corticosteroid that is used to relieve symptoms in several skin conditions that are characterised by inflammation such as eczema and insect bites. Pityriasis versicolor does not tend to cause significant skin inflammation so steroid creams are not appropriate.

Oral prednisolone

may be used to treat severe inflammatory or autoimmune skin conditions (e.g. severe eczema). It is not used for fungal infections like pityriasis versicolor.

Oral terbinafine

is an antifungal treatment used for dermatophyte infections such as onychomycosis or tinea corporis. It is not used in the treatment of pityriasis versicolor.

Topical clindamycin

is an antibiotic used for skin conditions that are associated with bacterial overgrowth (e.g. acne) and is not used to treat fungal skin infections.

question:
A 54-year-old Caucasian man presents with a rash on the face. He first noticed this four months ago when he experienced episodes of flushing on the face. This has often occurred after he had alcohol or in situations where he felt stressful. A month ago, he started noticing a rash on his cheeks which came on intermittently until two weeks ago when the rash has become permanent. There has been no pain or itch associated with the rash. He is otherwise fit and well. He does not smoke.

On examination of the face, there is marked erythema with papules, pustules and telangiectasia. There are no comedones seen. The rash is distributed across the cheeks and nose. There is no per-oral or peri-orbital involvement.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Rosacea features:

Acne rosacea

is the best fit for this patient because the clinical picture combines several cardinal features: episodic flushing precipitated by alcohol and emotional stress, fixed central facial erythema with telangiectasia, and later development of papules and pustules in the absence of comedones. These appearances, along with the typical anatomical distribution over the cheeks and nose, are classic for rosacea. Understanding that rosacea is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous unit helps explain why antibiotics such as doxycycline improve the inflammatory component while measures such as topical brimonidine target vasodilatation. Recognising these hallmarks is essential in primary care to initiate appropriate topical therapy, advise on trigger avoidance and use of high-factor sunscreen.

Systemic lupus erythematosus

can present with a malar or ‘butterfly’ rash but it is usually macular, non-scarring and photosensitive, and crucially spares the nasolabial folds. Papules, pustules and telangiectasia are uncommon in acute cutaneous lupus. Moreover, the patient has no systemic features such as arthralgia or constitutional upset, making SLE less likely.

Acne vulgaris

typically shows open and closed comedones as the first lesions, followed by inflammatory papules, pustules and nodules. Comedones are notably absent in this scenario, and adult-onset inflammatory acne without comedones is unusual. In addition, flushing episodes are not characteristic of acne vulgaris.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis

affects seborrhoeic areas – scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds and retro-auricular skin – and manifests as greasy, yellowish, scaling erythema rather than discrete papules and pustules. Telangiectasia and flushing are not prominent features, so the description does not correspond with seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Perioral dermatitis

presents with clusters of tiny papulopustules around the mouth, occasionally the peri-ocular skin, and typically spares a clear rim next to the vermilion border. In this patient, the eruption is centred on the cheeks and nose with no perioral involvement, making this diagnosis improbable. Unlike rosacea, perioral dermatitis is often associated with the use of topical corticosteroids, which is not mentioned here.

question: A 67-year-old man with a history of Parkinson's disease presents due to the development of an itchy, red rash on his neck, behind his ears and around the nasolabial folds. He had a similar flare up last winter but did not seek medical attention. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Parkinson's disease is associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis

The correct answer is

Seborrhoeic dermatitis

. This condition is a common, chronic or relapsing form of eczema/dermatitis that primarily affects sebum-gland rich areas including the scalp, face, and trunk. The presentation of an itchy, red rash on the neck, behind the ears and around the nasolabial folds in this patient is highly suggestive of Seborrhoeic dermatitis. Notably, Parkinson's disease patients have a higher incidence of seborrhoeic dermatitis due to increased sebum production.

Levodopa associated dermatitis

is incorrect as it typically presents as xerosis (dry skin) and pruritus without a distinct rash. It would also likely affect other parts of the body rather than being localised to sebum-rich areas.

Flexural psoriasis

is not correct because this type of psoriasis usually affects skin folds such as those found in the axillae or groin. It generally does not affect the face or scalp which are commonly involved in seborrhoeic dermatitis.

The option

Acne rosacea

is incorrect because rosacea typically presents with transient or persistent erythema, papules, pustules and telangiectasia on the face. Furthermore, rosacea does not cause itching which was one of the symptoms described by this patient.

Finally, a

Fixed drug reaction to ropinirole

, used in Parkinson's disease treatment, is unlikely because fixed drug reactions usually present as well-defined erythematous patches or plaques that recur at exactly the same site with each exposure to the drug. This patient had flare-ups during winter which suggests a seasonal influence rather than a constant exposure to medication.

question:
A 72-year-old woman presents with a several-month history of an ulcer overlying the medial aspect of the left leg. She has had chronic leg swelling for many years and a previous deep vein thrombosis in the same leg.

On examination, both legs are oedematous but the left is more than the right. A large, shallow ulcer is visible, superior to the medial malleolus; it does not look infected. There is some surrounding hyperpigmentation of the skin. Investigations are performed:


Ankle-brachial pressure index	1.1	(0.9 - 1.2)

Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?
explanation:
Management of venous ulceration - compression bandaging

The scenario describes a venous ulcer, given the history of chronic oedema, previous deep vein thrombosis and description of the ulcer. Given that the ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) is normal, arterial flow is not impaired and so first-line management involves the use of compression bandaging - usually four-layer. Compression bandaging has the strongest evidence base out of venous ulcer management options.

Compression stockings should be offered once the ulcer has healed, to prevent recurrence. They should not, however, be used immediately - compression bandaging should first be used.

Hydrocolloid dressings, and indeed other dressings, do not have much evidence to suggest benefit. Compression bandaging should instead be used.

Oral pentoxifylline is an effective adjunct to compression bandaging. It acts as a peripheral vasodilator, improving the healing rate. It is not first-line; bandaging is the correct option here and pentoxifylline may be used in addition to this.

Silver is an antimicrobial dressing. There is no evidence of infection here and so this would not be appropriate. Antimicrobial dressings are not routinely indicated in the management of venous ulcers.

question: A woman presents with painful erythematous lesions on her shins. Which one of the following is least associated with this presentation?

A 16-year-old female with a background of asthma is brought in by her concerned mother due to the appearance of a rash on her arm.

This came on overnight and is non-pruritic but slightly tender. The patient doesn't know how it could have happened - she denies using any new products or any history of trauma. Her mother also voices concerns about the child's school grades falling recently.

On examination, there are well demarcated linear lesions that form geometrical shapes on the left forearm and palmar aspect of the hand. The patient appears well, and examination is unremarkable otherwise.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Linear, well-demarcated skin lesions that appear suddenly, with 'la belle indifference'  → ?dermatitis artefacta

Dermatitis artefacta is the most likely diagnosis. It is a condition in which lesions are self-inflicted, usually owing to a psychological problem. It could be a form of deliberate self-harm or part of attention-seeking behaviour. Typically, it presents with skin lesions that are particularly geometrical (e.g. linear), appear overnight and in easily accessible areas (such as the limbs or face). These patients often deny causing the lesions themselves. The patient's grades have been falling, which could be a cause or a consequence of psychological difficulties, which may have led her to this particular type of self-harming behaviour.

Excoriated acne simply refers to acne that has been 'picked' at or scratched, causing excoriation of the skin. 'Acne excoriee des jeunes filles' is a type of neurotic or psychogenic excoriation. It is a reasonable differential in that the excoriation is self-inflicted. However, there is no mention of any signs of underlying acne (papules, comedones or pustules) to begin with, and it would be an unusual location for acne. Furthermore, patients with excoriated acne tend to admit that they pick it themselves, as opposed to patients with dermatitis artefacta.

Dermatitis herpetiformis would present with itchy blisters and raised red skin lesions, typically on the buttocks, elbows, knees, lower back and scalp of patients with coeliac disease. None of these features is present in this patient.

Eczema causes erythematous patches of skin that are often dry, itchy, cracked and/or sore. While it is an extremely common condition, it does not match the patient's presentation - eczema does not tend to cause geometric well-defined shapes or to appear overnight.

Eczema herpeticum is a rare but serious manifestation of herpes infection, typically occurring in young children with eczema or a history of atopy. It often requires admission. Although this child has asthma, nothing else in the history points to this diagnosis, and this teenager is not unwell.

question:
A 63-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a three-week history of an itchy rash over the face and upper chest. His only past medical history is HIV for which he is poorly compliant with his anti-retroviral medications.

On examination, areas of erythema over the eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and upper chest are noted. Excoriations surrounding the rash are present.

What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Seborrhoeic dermatitis - first-line treatment is topical ketoconazole

This man has presented with a rash consistent with seborrhoeic dermatitis, which he is at particular risk of given his past medical history of HIV. The first-line treatment for this condition is topical ketoconazole.

Oral fluconazole can be used to treat various fungal infections and has a role in antifungal prophylaxis in HIV however is not used in the treatment of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Oral prednisolone may be used in short courses to treat extensive inflammatory skin disease such as atopic dermatitis, however has no role in seborrhoeic dermatitis.

Topical steroids such as hydrocortisone can be used for short periods to treat seborrhoeic dermatitis however are not the most appropriate initial therapy.

UV therapy has a role in various skin diseases, notably psoriasis, however is not used in the management of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

question: A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with a persistent skin rash on his hands, arms, neck and face. The rash is red-brown in colour, symmetrical and scaly. He also complains of a poor appetite, nausea and diarrhoea. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely to have caused his symptoms?
explanation:
Niacin (B3) deficiency is characterised by dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia, a condition known as pellagra

The correct answer is

Niacin

. The patient's symptoms of a red-brown, symmetrical, scaly rash on the skin, poor appetite, nausea and diarrhoea are characteristic of pellagra, which is caused by a deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3). Niacin plays a crucial role in cellular metabolism and energy production. Chronic alcoholism can lead to malnutrition and poor absorption of essential vitamins and minerals, including niacin.

Folic acid

deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia with symptoms such as fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath and glossitis (inflammation of the tongue). Although alcoholics are at risk for folic acid deficiency due to malnutrition and poor absorption, the patient's symptoms do not fit this diagnosis.

A deficiency in

Thiamine

(vitamin B1) can result in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome or beriberi. Symptoms include peripheral neuropathy, muscle weakness, confusion, memory loss and ophthalmoplegia. While chronic alcoholism is a common cause of thiamine deficiency, the patient's presentation does not match these conditions.

Vitamin B6

(pyridoxine) deficiency may cause peripheral neuropathy, irritability and depression. However, these symptoms are not consistent with the patient's presentation.

Finally,

Zinc

deficiency can lead to dermatitis (skin inflammation), hair loss and immune dysfunction but does not fully explain the specific rash pattern described in this case.

question: A 55-year-old man presents with multiple erythematous target lesions two days after starting a new medication. Which one of the following drugs is most likely to have been started?
A 31-year-old woman develops with painful, purple lesions on her shins. Which one of the following medications is most likely to be responsible?

A 24-year-old woman presents due to a rash on her neck and forehead. She returned from a holiday in Cyprus 1 week ago and had her hair dyed 2 days ago. On examination there is a weepy, vesicular rash around her hairline although the scalp itself is not badly affected. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 45-year-old male with known HIV attends the genitourinary medicine clinic for a review.

A repeat CD4 count is taken:


CD4 count	197 cells/mm³ (500-1,400 cells/mm³)

The patient is started on co-trimoxazole, for prophylaxis against opportunistic infections, and continued on triple antiretroviral therapy of tenofovir, emtricitabine and raltegravir.

Eight days later the patient presents to the emergency department. He reports starting to feel generally unwell 3 days prior to his attendance with intermittent fevers and generalised myalgia. The patient also reports that he has developed a rash and sore eyes and lips in the last 24 hours.

On examination, the patient is found to have a tender area of erythema over the upper half of the torso with flaccid blistering of the skin. There is conjunctivitis in both eyes and tender blistering lesions are seen over the orobuccal mucosa.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mucosal involvement is prominent and severe in Stevens-Johnson syndrome

Patients with HIV can present with multiple different dermatological conditions. Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) is 100 times more common in patients with HIV. In this scenario, the patient was started on co-trimoxazole, a sulphonamide antibiotic, which is known to precipitate SJS. Presentations of SJS typically start within 1 week but can present up to one month after starting antibiotics. Where anticonvulsants are the causative agent, the presentation can be delayed by up to two months.

SJS presents initially with a prodromal illness of intermittent fevers, myalgia and a sore throat. After a few days, a painful, erythematous skin rash develops abruptly over the trunk and arms. Blisters then appear and merge to form sheets of detached skin. Mucosal involvement is prominent and severe with at least two mucosal surfaces becoming involved. In this case, the patient developed conjunctivitis and painful ulcerations on the lips.

Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense skin blistering and the mucosal surfaces are rarely involved. There is no increased association with HIV also.

Kaposi sarcoma is a condition more commonly seen in immunocompromised patients. It can present anywhere on the skin or mucosal surfaces, presenting initially as a painless erythematous lesion and can progress into painful ulcerations. The lesions are initially more discrete and present much more slowly than is reported here.

Pruritic papular eruption of HIV is a diagnosis of exclusion in patients with HIV presenting with a rash. Here there are other more likely differential diagnoses such as SJS. The condition can present at any time during HIV infection and presents with small erythematous papules which are intensely itchy. The mucosal surfaces are also spared.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome has been reported in the literature to occur in adult patients with HIV, however, this is extremely rare. It has a greater association in adults with chronic renal failure, but again this is still rare. This condition is typically seen in children under 5 years of age. The presentation is similar to SJS with a blistering, painful, erythematous skin rash extending over the body surfaces. Importantly, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome does not involve the mucosal surfaces, whereas SJS does.

question:
A 54-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a rash affecting her cheeks, nose, and forehead. The rash is worse when exposed to the sun. She has no past medical history.

On examination, there is an erythematous rash affecting her nose, cheeks, and forehead diffusely and involving the nasolabial folds. There is a minimal amount of papules and pustules visible.

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the first-line treatment?
explanation:
Rosacea treatment:

Topical ivermectin

is correct. The patient presents with an erythematous rash along with papules/pustules affecting her nose, cheeks, and forehead. This is typical of rosacea. The first line of management in mild-moderate cases is topical ivermectin. The underlying aetiology of rosacea is complex and yet to be entirely elucidated. There is a probable multifactorial aetiology to the disease including immune and vascular dysfunction, neurogenic dysregulation, presence of cutaneous microorganisms, ultraviolet damage, and skin barrier dysfunction. Ivermectin is postulated to have an anti-inflammatory and anti-parasitic effect, targeting cutaneous organisms like Demodex mites.

Oral doxycycline

is incorrect. This can be used in combination with topical ivermectin in severe cases of rosacea. It has anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic properties that make it useful in the treatment of rosacea.

Oral hydroxychloroquine

is incorrect. This is an anti-malarial used in the management of systemic lupus erythematosus. It can be used for the skin manifestations of the disease. Malar rash affecting the cheeks and nose in lupus tends to spare the nasolabial folds, which are involved in this case.

Oral lymecycline

is incorrect. This is an option for the treatment of acne. However, erythema in acne tends to be local to the papules/pustules rather than diffusely affecting a wider area like in rosacea. Therefore, rosacea is the more likely diagnosis in this case.

Topical steroids

are incorrect. This can be used for a wide variety of inflammatory skin disorders (although should be minimised on the face where possible). It is not the first-line treatment of rosacea, which is the most likely diagnosis here.

question:
A 40-year-old woman visits the GP with a two-month history of unintentional weight loss. She reports feeling more fatigued than usual but otherwise has no localising signs or symptoms. On examination, hyperpigmentation and thickening of the skin in her groin and axilla are noted; the patient believes this has also been present for approximately 2 months.

Which malignancy is most associated with this presentation?
options: Ductal cell carcinoma of the breast
explanation:
The most common malignancy associated with acanthosis nigricans

This presentation is consistent with a diagnosis of acanthosis nigricans. Although a multitude of benign conditions such as hyperinsulinaemia and obesity can cause this, 90% of malignant causes of acanthosis nigrans are gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma.

Ductal cell carcinoma of the breast is associated with extramammary Paget's disease.

Gastric squamous cell carcinoma is most associated with acrokeratosis paraneoplastica, in regards to cutaneous manifestations.

Multiple myeloma can cause pityriasis rotunda but is seldom a cause of acanthosis nigricans.

Pancreatic carcinoma is associated with superficial thrombophlebitis also known as Trousseau syndrome.

question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with an itchy papular rash on her palms, extending onto the flexor aspect of the forearms. White lines are visible across the surface of the rash. Where she has scratched at the lesions she has noticed a worsening of the rash. On examination, there is also thinning of the nails with longitudinal ridges visible.

What treatment would be most appropriate first-line?
explanation:
Potent topical steroids are the first-line treatment for lichen planus

The correct answer is

potent topical steroids

. This woman's presentation is consistent with lichen planus, and potent topical steroids are therefore first-line.

Emollients

are not indicated in the treatment of lichen planus. They are used widely in the treatment of skin conditions such as eczema and psoriasis.

Oral steroids

may be indicated in cases with particularly extensive or refractory disease.

Calcipotriol

is a synthetic vitamin D derivative used in the treatment of psoriasis, rather than lichen planus. It helps reduce scale in psoriatic plaques. Common side effects include burning or stinging on application, and skin itching and dryness.

Fusidic acid

is used to treat staphylococcal skin infections, such as impetigo. Fusidic acid is a fusidane - this group of antibiotics inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to factor G, disrupting energy supply to the synthesis process.

question:
A 48-year-old man presents with skin lesions that have been ongoing for the past 3 months. This started with frequent ulcers forming along the buccal mucosa and hard palate. Over the past 1 month, his skin had become increasingly pruritic with erosions appearing over the surface of his chest and back. He also noticed blisters over these areas that would be pruritic.

On examination, erosions over the chest and back were seen with several crusted lesions noted. Small flaccid vesicles measuring 1-2cm were also seen scattered randomly across his torso. Ulcers within the buccal mucosa and gums were also noted.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Blisters/bullae

Pemphigus vulgaris is the likely diagnosis due to the presence of flaccid vesicles and mucosal involvement. It commonly affects patients from the age of 30-60. Erosions are a common presenting complaint as the thin, flaccid vesicles will easily rupture with friction.

Bullous pemphigoid is unlikely in this case as this typically presents with tense bullae. Mucosal involvement should not be seen if this was the underlying diagnosis.

Linear IgA dermatosis is less likely in this case as the pattern of distribution of the vesicles will be annular/targetoid in this condition. Linear IgA dermatosis also more commonly presents in either teenage years or during the 6th decade of life, making the diagnosis less likely.

Erythema multiforme is not the diagnosis in this case as this will typically present with a targetoid rash and a precipitant such as an underlying infection or medication is normally found. Erosions and ulcers within the oral mucosa can also be seen.

Dermatitis herpetiformis typically presents with small vesicles along the extensor surfaces that are intensely itchy. It is not associated with the formation of bullae.

question:
An 18-year-old man presents with a 4-year history of recurrent nosebleeds. On examination, he has multiple telangiectasias in his oral cavity. You suspect a diagnosis of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.

What option best describes the inheritance pattern of this condition?
explanation:
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia - autosomal dominant

This case presents a patient with suspected hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome. HHT is an inherited condition characterized by an

autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance and age-related penetrance

, with the majority of individuals manifesting symptoms such as recurrent epistaxis (nosebleeds) during adolescence.

In cases where HHT is suspected, it is imperative to conduct a family history and consider referral for genetic testing. Most cases are attributable to mutations in the endoglin or ACVRLK1 genes, though mutations in other genes, including SMAD4, RASA1, and BMPR9, may also be causative.

It is essential to understand that HHT follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern; it does not conform to

autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant, or X-linked recessive

patterns.

The term

anticipation

refers to the phenomenon where a condition will present itself at a younger age with each successive generation. This phenomenon is not observed in HHT.
